titles.title: Assessing upper bounds for solar-powered Controlled Environment Agriculture on existing cropland

descriptions.description:
Main data and methods used for Roberts et al. (2026) - "Assessing upper bounds for solar-powered Controlled Environment Agriculture on existing cropland"

Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems 10:1945186

 

Methods -

CEA energy demand model setup

To compare CEA powered by PV with crop-specific production globally, we derived a spatially-explicit energy demand per CEA. This type of comparison has been addressed in localized contexts in Weidner et al.[19], but lack a global scope as indicated in Bomford[23], Righini et al.[24,37], and Stanghellini & Katzin[27]. While there are many different greenhouse production models available[38], the specific aim of this study was to examine CEA systems and energy use on a global scale and this led to the construction of a model to address this aim. We developed a simple mechanistic model similar to the Van Henten model[39,40] as a way of incorporating experimental CEA crop production values and parameters[24] across a global spatial array (Supplementary Fig. 2). In order to make the model globally applicable, we made certain elements more generalized than they might be in a site-specific model, such as the building design, crop growing parameters and production system, building interaction with outside conditions, and the indoor environment control systems.

The CEA yields, harvest metrics, and light requirements were taken directly from Righini et al.[24]. In that study, the authors compiled and analysed CEA metrics across multiple studies as well as their own experiments for wheat[28–30], soybean[24], potato[28,31,32], and tomato[24]. CEA aims to homogenize crop outputs and yields regardless of the geographic location, seasons, and local growing conditions. We applied this assumption to our model and kept CEA yields constant for each crop across the global spatial array. The yields from individual studies in Righini et al.[24] were analysed for parameters such as light requirements (photoperiod and photosynthetic photon flux density (PPFD)), the growing cycle length (days), and the resulting yields in terms of plant density, harvest index (ratio of harvested biomass to total plant biomass), fresh harvest yield per growing cycle, dry harvest yield per cycle, and annual fresh weight yield (as the sum of multiple growing cycles possible per year). The values from that study used in this CEA energy model are listed in Supplementary Table 2. Long-term and continuous datasets on CEA for different crops such as those included in this study were not available. Hence, we extrapolated from the experimental results that were available to assume multiple yields per year (3-4) that would be possible given the reported growing production times and days to harvest. The reference experimental studies all used soilless growing set-ups (e.g., hydroponic), so the same is assumed in our modelled CEA. Mills[34] also compared energy demands across CEA studies and found differences between and across crop types. Mills[34] acknowledges that for crops such as wheat, few studies are available and in some cases, there is a reliance on modelled crop simulations. Given the discrepancies and potentially large ranges between crops and individual studies, we chose to directly apply the RIghini et al. CEA data compilation as the main source of crop specific parameters.

Two types of CEA were evaluated, a high-tech closed greenhouse (GH) and a vertical farm (VF), to model the energy required for each set-up to achieve the target yields as compiled in Righini et al.[24]. The mechanistic greenhouse model assumed uniform internal conditions, also known as a “perfectly stirred tank”[39], and considered water vapour and energy balances in a similar way to the Van Henten model[38–40] (Supplementary Tables 1 & 3). 

We adapted the basic greenhouse balance equations for energy and water vapour from the van Henten model[39,40] to run the simplified model on global scales to calculate the CEA energy demand:

 dE/dt  = QSun + QHeat + QLamp - QVent - QLatent - QCon – QFIR – Qcool   (J m-2 s-1 = W m-2)

dMW/dt = WTrans + WEvap + WHum - WCond - WVent - WDehum     (kg {water vapor} m-2  s-1)

dE/dt = net change of energy

Q = rate of heat transfer from the various factors, inside and outside the growing space

dMW/dt = net change of water mass

W = rate of water vapor change over time from inside and outside factors

More detailed processes can be captured in van Henten[39,40] or other greenhouse models[38]; however, to represent the major drivers of energy use, we only focused on these specific aspects. The process for calculating the influence of solar radiation was the same for both GH and VF and was an adapted version of the equation[24]:

 

Energy Uselights = PPFD * photoperiod * 3600 * ηlights *10-6 (MJ m-2 day-1)

 

 ηlights= electrical efficacy

 

The walls in the VF had 0% light entering, whereas the GH had 82% of solar radiation entering the growing space[22]. For incoming solar radiation, the daily total values were per month for an average daily solar radiation (J m-2 day-1). This incoming average daily solar radiation load was converted to a PPFD (μmol m-2 s-1) as the total daily PPFD or Daily Light Interval (DLI) as mol m-2 day-1. The PPFD and photoperiod for each crop from Righini et al.[24] was converted into a DLI requirement per day. The difference between the actual DLI and this required DLI indicated the lighting (J m-2 day-1) shortfall. Dividing this shortfall by the electrical efficacy*16 of the lights gave the average daily supplemental lighting demand (MJ m-2 day-1) for each month of 2020. 

While there are other potential processes or factors that would contribute to CEA energy demand, such as water pumps and irrigation, mechanized automation, and computer and sensor controls, these are relatively minor compared to the major energy drivers such as supplemental lighting, growing space heating and cooling, and ventilation[24]. 

Between the two CEA set-ups, there were minor adjustments to the building dimensions, crop growing area, and wall insulation properties. The simplified building designs similar to Weidner et al.[19,41] were intended to capture the basic parameters of the indoor growing space and basic interactions with the outdoor environment. In this way, the major drivers of CEA energy demand could be compared while avoiding specific building designs that vary by specific location and use. In this simulation, the vertical farm and closed greenhouse each had supplemental lighting, temperature, and humidity controls to maintain the same light requirements, indoor conditions, and annual yields depending on the crop requirements. 

The model considered a 1 ha GH (75% of the building footprint is considered usable as growing area) and a 0.25 ha VF (with 4 stacked layers that utilize 75% of the building footprint for growing area). The VF yield was assumed to be four times per hectare of building footprint compared to the GH as a way to capture the increased production capacity potential for the VF. Additionally, the VF was assumed to be 8m in height and the GH was assumed to be 4m in height. The same indoor environment was assumed for both systems and in turn the capacity to maintain that growing space environment is what drives the energy demand (Supplementary Table 1 & 3). 

We used the average daily light (PPFD) requirements, photoperiod, and annual yields according to Righini et al.[24] and included updated lighting and indoor environmental parameters to meet the best available standards for LEDs and heat pumps (Supplementary Table 4). The values presented by Righini et al.[24] include their own data for tomato and soybean experiments as well as a compilation of previous experiments for wheat[28–30] and potato[28,31,32] trials. Each of the selected experiments may have differed in specific CEA designs; however, all were soilless systems that relied entirely on supplemental lighting for crop growth. The mechanistic greenhouse model had a time-step of one day for all indoor processes. The outdoor climate conditions were averaged for each month and recorded as the average daily temperature, relative humidity, and solar radiation flux for each grid cell per month. The model received the daily average (for each month) as input data and first calculated the influence of the outside factors on the indoor growing parameters (temperature, relative humidity, and light) for both VF and GH. Then for each growing space parameter, the corresponding CEA component was forced to correct the factor to bring it back into the target range. For heating and cooling this was done with a heat pump, for relative humidity with humidifier or ventilation, and LEDs for supplemental lighting. 

The energy requirement for each component to maintain the target growing conditions was summed for each average day per month. These daily energy totals were multiplied by the number of days per month to return a monthly energy demand based on the average day in that month. These monthly values were then summed to return an annual energy demand. This annual energy demand was divided by the annual CEA yield per building to give the energy use efficiency (MJ kg-1) for each crop and CEA system.

The resulting energy demand reflects the energy needed to maintain those constant internal conditions within the target ranges. By doing this, we were able to compare the plant specific growing parameters and yields from Righini et al.[24] between VF and GH systems.

 

CEA energy demand simulation inputs

The selected crops for the study were wheat, potato, soybean, and tomato to represent grain, legume, tuber, and vegetable crop types. The temperature control (15-23°C) and relative humidity range (60-85%) were set at levels similar to Weidner et al.[19,41] (Supplementary Table 3) We assumed a fixed biomass production per growing cycle and year (yield biomass per m2 and harvest index adapted from Righini et al.[24] instead of simulating crop growth over time and across growth stages. Because evapotranspiration is a complex process that varies between crops and plant stages, we applied a single generalised evapotranspiration rate of 4.5 mm day-1 for all crops[42–44]. Additionally, the energy to power water pumps and recirculation is relatively insignificant compared to other CEA processes and the water use itself might be over 90% lower (for both closed greenhouses and vertical farms) than comparable field systems[20,24,45]. For this reason, water use and energy for the irrigation and water pump and recirculation system were not included.

A heat pump is used to maintain the internal temperature within the target range with a Coefficient of Performance, for heating, (COP) of 4.0 and an Energy Efficiency Ratio, for cooling, (EER) of 13.0[46]. These COP and EER are general values in order to reflect that these efficiencies could be influenced by local conditions and product designs. The building wall insulation R-value was kept at 3 for the GH[47] and 15 for the VF[48]. Supplemental lighting from LEDs was set to 3.5 mmol J-1 to represent the current best available standard[22,27] (Supplementary Table 4).

ERA 5 Agrometeorological environmental data[49] (0.1° x 0.1° resolution) were used for daily measurements for solar radiation flux (J m-2), temperature (K at 2m height), and relative humidity (% at 2m height at 12h) for the year 2020. The daily values for each grid cell were averaged for each month in the year 2020. This averaged daily value per month for the climate parameters (solar radiation, temperature, relative humidity) were input into the CEA energy demand model at 1-day time steps. The use of a monthly averaged value for each climate factor was a trade-off to run the model efficiently on a global array while still capturing site and seasonal variations. The model outputs were calculated in total energy demand (MJ) per day and then summed for a monthly and annual total. The annual energy demand to crop yield (MJ kg-1) or energy use efficiency in each CEA system was then calculated per grid cell. Both monthly energy demand and annual energy use efficiency were downscaled to a 1km grid in order to compare to the higher resolution land use and solar PV potential model outputs. The resulting energy use efficiency as MJ kg-1 for each crop calculated by region for both CEA systems is shown in Fig. 2.

 

Global crop area, yield, and production

We used a data harmonisation approach based on the HILDA+ land use reconstruction model[2], to allocate 2020 crop production (t km-2) and crop harvest area (ha km-2) for the target crops to a 1km global grid array. This approach allowed us to harmonise the outputs of multiple crop models, datasets, and statistical inventories to produce crop area, yield, and production maps for each target crop. In HILDA+, the cropland areas were isolated and used to mask the CROPGRIDS crop-specific crop area data (reference year 2020)[36]. GAEZ v4 (reference year 2015)[35], along with the statistical data for FAO country level harvest area and production quantity totals (reference year 2020)[50] were used to assign the pixel-level harvest area (ha) and yields (t/ha) for the target crops. 

This was done by first normalizing the GAEZ v4 crop yield values, i.e. dividing them by their national and cropland-wide mean, as well as normalizing the CROPGRIDS crop area values by their national and cropland-wide sum (all constrained by HILDA+ cropland and at least 5% CROPGRIDS crop coverage). This normalization was done in order to align each input dataset with the same consistent spatial array and projection. The normalized values, crop yield and area, were then multiplied by FAO crop yield and harvested area in 2020, respectively. The crop production (t) was finally derived by a pixel-based multiplication of country- and crop-specific yield (t ha-1) and harvested areas (ha). Each crop then had a specific harvest area (ha), yield (t ha-1), and production (t) per grid cell for the year 2020. In order to harmonise these different datasets, steps were taken to minimise inter-dataset variability. FAO statistics only report crop area harvested, which could include multiple harvests on the same area, so the CROPGRIDS crop cultivation area layer was used to set a fraction of crop area per grid cell prior to allocating the FAO area harvested within each country’s grid cells. Upper thresholds for crop area were set to limit any instance where the area from multiple harvests were applied to the same grid cell. In this way we were able to remove inconsistencies or data artifacts that would otherwise inflate the crop area beyond what was available in the grid cell (i.e., more than 100 ha crop area for a 100 ha grid cell). The data harmonisation process of crop area, yield, and production is simplified in Supplementary Fig. 4.

 

PV-powered CEA comparison with 2020 crop area, yield, and production

The CEA crop yields[24] were kept constant across the global array in order to test the area and PV energy capacity to scale these experimental values globally. The multiple datasets[35,36,50] used across the analysis reported the reference yields and production in harvested biomass. For this reason, we used CEA production and yield values for harvested biomass. For different research questions, this metric could be changed to dry harvest weight, calories, or other specific nutritional or agronomic units. The first step to calculate the comparison against 2020 crop production was to determine the CEA building area needed to meet 2020 production (t km-2) per grid cell. The annual CEA yields were calculated per growing area and were set per grid cell to reflect the CEA systems (0.75ha growing area per 1ha GH building area and 0.75ha growing area per 0.25ha VF building area). The 2020 production array was divided by the annual CEA yield (per growing area) per crop to give the CEA building area needed for year-round CEA production in each grid cell. This CEA footprint requirement was summed per hectare for GH or per 0.25 hectare for VF per grid cell.

To calculate the solar PV area needed for the CEA, the monthly solar PV potential (kWh m-2) was derived from Saxena et al.[33]. The area available for PV per grid cell was calculated as the harvest area subtracted by the CEA building area per grid cell. The surface area coverage of the solar PV was assumed to be 75% of a given area[22], so the potential energy available to the CEA was reduced by this factor. This PV potential was then multiplied by an efficiency factor[51] (26.8%) for conversion to usable electricity. The total CEA energy demand per building (1ha for GH and 0.25ha for VF) per grid cell was multiplied by the CEA building area requirement to calculate the total CEA energy demand per grid cell. The monthly PV area requirement to directly power the CEA was calculated by multiplying the potential PV energy by the CEA energy demand per grid cell. The process is summarized visually in Supplementary Fig. 3 and all CEA component inputs are summarized in Supplementary Tables 1-4.

For year-round production, the month with the greatest PV area requirement for each grid cell became the fixed PV area needed to power the required CEA area for that grid cell. No energy storage was assumed from one day to the next, so each day had only the monthly 1-day average to fulfil the CEA demand. We also analysed continuous 9-month CEA production capacity as a way to reduce the energy demand and the required PV area to power the CEA. The reduction in yield capacity was taken into account and the CEA area needed to meet 2020-Production per grid cell was re-calculated. For the shortened 9-month production cycle, the 9-month stretch with the lowest PV area requirements to meet indoor energy demands were calculated per grid cell. Similar to the year-round production, the month with the greatest PV area requirement for this 9-month cycle, determined the PV area needed for that grid cell. The resulting area (ha) of PV needed to power a year-round or 9-month CEA is displayed spatially in Supplementary Fig. 7.

This CEA building area plus PV area was the total area that was then compared to the crop harvest area per grid cell. The land area requirement balance (ha) was calculated by subtracting the CEA building footprint plus PV area from the crop area per grid cell. If the area balance was negative, then not enough area was available for the CEA-PV to meet 2020 production in that grid cell. If the balance was zero or positive, the CEA-PV matched 2020 production and any positive value could be considered a lower required land area than 2020 production area in ha. 

Only the grid cells with a positive area balance were used to calculate the potential extra or surplus production by allowing the model to utilise all crop area available and CEA production above 2020 production values. This extra-production was calculated by incrementally adding CEA units (1ha for GH and 0.25ha for VF) and the required PV area per building. This process was done iteratively until the crop harvest area in that grid cell reached zero. The sum of this extra production according to the CEA building area added, was then added to that grid cell total production quantity. The spatial distribution of areas where CEA met 2020 production can be seen in Fig. 3. The global totals and comparison between CEA systems for harvest area (ha) where CEA met 2020 production, production quantity (t) met by CEA, lower CEA-PV land area requirements compared to 2020 production (ha), and extra production (t) by CEA are given in Fig. 4. The regional breakdowns relative to the global totals as well as the breakdown within each region are given in Supplementary Figs. 8&9.

 

Yield gap analysis

The yield gap analysis and comparison were done to apply a single metric for comparing crop production challenges globally. For this study we used the GAEZ v4 crop-wise Yield Achievement Ratio[35] (YAR) global gridded (5 arc minutes) dataset for the most recent average (2009-2011). The YAR was calculated by GAEZ as the ratio of actual (average) yields to the attainable yields for each grid cell. The attainable yields were calculated as the biophysical influences (e.g., solar radiation, water, nutrients, temperature) on yield (potential yield) while considering location specific constraints (e.g., soil or terrain, pest pressure, management). For the crops analysed in this study, GAEZ only has YAR data for wheat, soybean, and potato, so we limited the yield gap analysis to these crops. The ratio of actual/ attainable yields is inversely proportional to the yield gap, as a higher ratio indicates a smaller yield gap. 

We used the GAEZ YAR data that had already been divided into bins corresponding to the crop-wise YAR. The 2020 crop-wise harvest area (ha) was compared to the corresponding YAR to calculate the distribution of crop harvest area per YAR bin. This distribution (percent of harvest area (ha)) per YAR bin was plotted to complement the global YAR maps plotted directly from the GAEZ dataset.

CEA-PV system performance compared to 2020 production was then evaluated against the reference crop yield gaps. Only grid cells where there was spatial agreement between the CROPGRIDS and GAEZ YAR datasets were considered. To analyse CEA-PV relationships with crop yield gaps, only the grid cells where CEA-PV demonstrated the ability to meet 2020 production were considered. Including only these CEA-PV net area positive areas was done to focus on the technical potential of CEA in alleviating yield gap constraints. In our analysis, CEA-PV net negative could not meet the same production values as 2020 production without additional crop area, it was assumed that CEA in these areas would be able to aid in yield gap closures. The area (ha) that was net positive CEA-PV crop area was summed for each YAR bin and the percent of the net positive CEA-PV crop area was plotted alongside the total crop harvest area distribution. Supplementary Fig. 1 provides a general overview of the yield gap analysis process.

 

Electricity grid constraints

The Arderne et al.[52] electrical grid dataset was used to evaluate the current electrical grid coverage in areas that overlap with areas that meet 2020 production (CEA-PV technical capacity areas). Where there was at least medium-voltage electricity, a 2km buffer was set as the maximum distance for connection to these electricity grids. The grid cells where there was overlap of this grid network and buffer with these CEA-PV grid cells that met 2020 production were summed, as well as those that were outside of this 2km buffer. The grid cells were then multiplied by the crop harvest area (ha) in that grid cell and then summed crop at the country- and regional-levels. The proportion of harvest area (ha) where CEA met 2020 production within the 2km electricity grid was then calculated for country and region as seen in Fig. 5. The spatial overlap of areas where CEA met 2020 production and the electricity grid can be seen in Supplementary Fig. 10.

 

Aridity Index

The Global Aridity Index Database as described in Zomer et al.(52) was used to compare where CEA matched 2020 production against aridity zones. The aridity index was divided into bins according to the index value. These index values were overlaid on the grid cells where CEA matched 2020 production. The harvest area (ha) was then multiplied by the number of grid cells within each index bin. The harvest area (ha) where CEA matched 2020 production was plotted according to the aridity index bin and results are given in Supplementary Fig. 11.

 

Model assumption sensitivity

            A deterministic sensitivity analysis was conducted to evaluate CEA-PV equivalent capacity reactions to changes in model assumptions. The sensitivity analysis evaluated changing assumptions around three parameters directly influencing CEA-PV area requirements and subsequent equivalent-capacity calculations: CEA crop yield, CEA energy demand, and PV conversion efficiency. Changes to each assumption were considered individually and for their combined effects on CEA-PV equivalent capacity. The main “baseline” analysis for GH and VF applied the experimental CEA yields described above and calculated the CEA building area required to match 2020 crop production in each grid cell, while the PV area requirement was determined from the corresponding CEA energy demand and a baseline PV conversion efficiency of 26.8%.

For the yield sensitivity analysis, the annual CEA yield for each crop was reduced by 10%, 25%, and 50%. The required CEA building area was then recalculated directly from 2020 crop production using the reduced yield while retaining the same GH- or VF-specific growing areas and corresponding year-round or 9-month growing cycles. The greater CEA area required under lower yields also increased growing area and associated PV area requirements to match 2020 crop production. For the energy sensitivity, CEA energy demand per unit growing area was increased by 10%, 25%, and 50%, while CEA yields and building area requirements were maintained at baseline input values. In turn, the corresponding PV area requirement increased to meet the increased energy demand. For the PV efficiency sensitivity, conversion efficiency was reduced from the baseline input value of 26.8% to 22%, while CEA crop yields and energy demands were kept constant. The PV area requirements were then required to provide the same amount of energy to meet CEA energy demands.

Additionally, the joint effects of combining CEA yield reductions, energy demand increases, and PV conversion efficiency reductions were evaluated. For each joint effect scenario, the revised CEA building area and PV requirements were compared to the available crop-wise harvested area in each grid cell using the same approach as the baseline analysis to calculate equivalent capacity. The sensitivity analysis tested the change in absolute area (ha), production (t), and less crop area required (ha) and corresponding global percentages for the CEA systems, year-round and 9-month growing cycles, and four crops. The sensitivity analysis therefore tested how these CEA systems performed under less favourable model assumptions rather than representing probabilistic uncertainty ranges.

titles.title: Assessing upper bounds for solar-powered Controlled Environment Agriculture on existing cropland

descriptions.description:
Main data and methods used for Roberts et al. (2026) - "Assessing upper bounds for solar-powered Controlled Environment Agriculture on existing cropland"

Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems 10:1945186

 

Methods -

CEA energy demand model setup

To compare CEA powered by PV with crop-specific production globally, we derived a spatially-explicit energy demand per CEA. This type of comparison has been addressed in localized contexts in Weidner et al.[19], but lack a global scope as indicated in Bomford[23], Righini et al.[24,37], and Stanghellini & Katzin[27]. While there are many different greenhouse production models available[38], the specific aim of this study was to examine CEA systems and energy use on a global scale and this led to the construction of a model to address this aim. We developed a simple mechanistic model similar to the Van Henten model[39,40] as a way of incorporating experimental CEA crop production values and parameters[24] across a global spatial array (Supplementary Fig. 2). In order to make the model globally applicable, we made certain elements more generalized than they might be in a site-specific model, such as the building design, crop growing parameters and production system, building interaction with outside conditions, and the indoor environment control systems.

The CEA yields, harvest metrics, and light requirements were taken directly from Righini et al.[24]. In that study, the authors compiled and analysed CEA metrics across multiple studies as well as their own experiments for wheat[28–30], soybean[24], potato[28,31,32], and tomato[24]. CEA aims to homogenize crop outputs and yields regardless of the geographic location, seasons, and local growing conditions. We applied this assumption to our model and kept CEA yields constant for each crop across the global spatial array. The yields from individual studies in Righini et al.[24] were analysed for parameters such as light requirements (photoperiod and photosynthetic photon flux density (PPFD)), the growing cycle length (days), and the resulting yields in terms of plant density, harvest index (ratio of harvested biomass to total plant biomass), fresh harvest yield per growing cycle, dry harvest yield per cycle, and annual fresh weight yield (as the sum of multiple growing cycles possible per year). The values from that study used in this CEA energy model are listed in Supplementary Table 2. Long-term and continuous datasets on CEA for different crops such as those included in this study were not available. Hence, we extrapolated from the experimental results that were available to assume multiple yields per year (3-4) that would be possible given the reported growing production times and days to harvest. The reference experimental studies all used soilless growing set-ups (e.g., hydroponic), so the same is assumed in our modelled CEA. Mills[34] also compared energy demands across CEA studies and found differences between and across crop types. Mills[34] acknowledges that for crops such as wheat, few studies are available and in some cases, there is a reliance on modelled crop simulations. Given the discrepancies and potentially large ranges between crops and individual studies, we chose to directly apply the RIghini et al. CEA data compilation as the main source of crop specific parameters.

Two types of CEA were evaluated, a high-tech closed greenhouse (GH) and a vertical farm (VF), to model the energy required for each set-up to achieve the target yields as compiled in Righini et al.[24]. The mechanistic greenhouse model assumed uniform internal conditions, also known as a “perfectly stirred tank”[39], and considered water vapour and energy balances in a similar way to the Van Henten model[38–40] (Supplementary Tables 1 & 3). 

We adapted the basic greenhouse balance equations for energy and water vapour from the van Henten model[39,40] to run the simplified model on global scales to calculate the CEA energy demand:

 dE/dt  = QSun + QHeat + QLamp - QVent - QLatent - QCon – QFIR – Qcool   (J m-2 s-1 = W m-2)

dMW/dt = WTrans + WEvap + WHum - WCond - WVent - WDehum     (kg {water vapor} m-2  s-1)

dE/dt = net change of energy

Q = rate of heat transfer from the various factors, inside and outside the growing space

dMW/dt = net change of water mass

W = rate of water vapor change over time from inside and outside factors

More detailed processes can be captured in van Henten[39,40] or other greenhouse models[38]; however, to represent the major drivers of energy use, we only focused on these specific aspects. The process for calculating the influence of solar radiation was the same for both GH and VF and was an adapted version of the equation[24]:

 

Energy Uselights = PPFD * photoperiod * 3600 * ηlights *10-6 (MJ m-2 day-1)

 

 ηlights= electrical efficacy

 

The walls in the VF had 0% light entering, whereas the GH had 82% of solar radiation entering the growing space[22]. For incoming solar radiation, the daily total values were per month for an average daily solar radiation (J m-2 day-1). This incoming average daily solar radiation load was converted to a PPFD (μmol m-2 s-1) as the total daily PPFD or Daily Light Interval (DLI) as mol m-2 day-1. The PPFD and photoperiod for each crop from Righini et al.[24] was converted into a DLI requirement per day. The difference between the actual DLI and this required DLI indicated the lighting (J m-2 day-1) shortfall. Dividing this shortfall by the electrical efficacy*16 of the lights gave the average daily supplemental lighting demand (MJ m-2 day-1) for each month of 2020. 

While there are other potential processes or factors that would contribute to CEA energy demand, such as water pumps and irrigation, mechanized automation, and computer and sensor controls, these are relatively minor compared to the major energy drivers such as supplemental lighting, growing space heating and cooling, and ventilation[24]. 

Between the two CEA set-ups, there were minor adjustments to the building dimensions, crop growing area, and wall insulation properties. The simplified building designs similar to Weidner et al.[19,41] were intended to capture the basic parameters of the indoor growing space and basic interactions with the outdoor environment. In this way, the major drivers of CEA energy demand could be compared while avoiding specific building designs that vary by specific location and use. In this simulation, the vertical farm and closed greenhouse each had supplemental lighting, temperature, and humidity controls to maintain the same light requirements, indoor conditions, and annual yields depending on the crop requirements. 

The model considered a 1 ha GH (75% of the building footprint is considered usable as growing area) and a 0.25 ha VF (with 4 stacked layers that utilize 75% of the building footprint for growing area). The VF yield was assumed to be four times per hectare of building footprint compared to the GH as a way to capture the increased production capacity potential for the VF. Additionally, the VF was assumed to be 8m in height and the GH was assumed to be 4m in height. The same indoor environment was assumed for both systems and in turn the capacity to maintain that growing space environment is what drives the energy demand (Supplementary Table 1 & 3). 

We used the average daily light (PPFD) requirements, photoperiod, and annual yields according to Righini et al.[24] and included updated lighting and indoor environmental parameters to meet the best available standards for LEDs and heat pumps (Supplementary Table 4). The values presented by Righini et al.[24] include their own data for tomato and soybean experiments as well as a compilation of previous experiments for wheat[28–30] and potato[28,31,32] trials. Each of the selected experiments may have differed in specific CEA designs; however, all were soilless systems that relied entirely on supplemental lighting for crop growth. The mechanistic greenhouse model had a time-step of one day for all indoor processes. The outdoor climate conditions were averaged for each month and recorded as the average daily temperature, relative humidity, and solar radiation flux for each grid cell per month. The model received the daily average (for each month) as input data and first calculated the influence of the outside factors on the indoor growing parameters (temperature, relative humidity, and light) for both VF and GH. Then for each growing space parameter, the corresponding CEA component was forced to correct the factor to bring it back into the target range. For heating and cooling this was done with a heat pump, for relative humidity with humidifier or ventilation, and LEDs for supplemental lighting. 

The energy requirement for each component to maintain the target growing conditions was summed for each average day per month. These daily energy totals were multiplied by the number of days per month to return a monthly energy demand based on the average day in that month. These monthly values were then summed to return an annual energy demand. This annual energy demand was divided by the annual CEA yield per building to give the energy use efficiency (MJ kg-1) for each crop and CEA system.

The resulting energy demand reflects the energy needed to maintain those constant internal conditions within the target ranges. By doing this, we were able to compare the plant specific growing parameters and yields from Righini et al.[24] between VF and GH systems.

 

CEA energy demand simulation inputs

The selected crops for the study were wheat, potato, soybean, and tomato to represent grain, legume, tuber, and vegetable crop types. The temperature control (15-23°C) and relative humidity range (60-85%) were set at levels similar to Weidner et al.[19,41] (Supplementary Table 3) We assumed a fixed biomass production per growing cycle and year (yield biomass per m2 and harvest index adapted from Righini et al.[24] instead of simulating crop growth over time and across growth stages. Because evapotranspiration is a complex process that varies between crops and plant stages, we applied a single generalised evapotranspiration rate of 4.5 mm day-1 for all crops[42–44]. Additionally, the energy to power water pumps and recirculation is relatively insignificant compared to other CEA processes and the water use itself might be over 90% lower (for both closed greenhouses and vertical farms) than comparable field systems[20,24,45]. For this reason, water use and energy for the irrigation and water pump and recirculation system were not included.

A heat pump is used to maintain the internal temperature within the target range with a Coefficient of Performance, for heating, (COP) of 4.0 and an Energy Efficiency Ratio, for cooling, (EER) of 13.0[46]. These COP and EER are general values in order to reflect that these efficiencies could be influenced by local conditions and product designs. The building wall insulation R-value was kept at 3 for the GH[47] and 15 for the VF[48]. Supplemental lighting from LEDs was set to 3.5 mmol J-1 to represent the current best available standard[22,27] (Supplementary Table 4).

ERA 5 Agrometeorological environmental data[49] (0.1° x 0.1° resolution) were used for daily measurements for solar radiation flux (J m-2), temperature (K at 2m height), and relative humidity (% at 2m height at 12h) for the year 2020. The daily values for each grid cell were averaged for each month in the year 2020. This averaged daily value per month for the climate parameters (solar radiation, temperature, relative humidity) were input into the CEA energy demand model at 1-day time steps. The use of a monthly averaged value for each climate factor was a trade-off to run the model efficiently on a global array while still capturing site and seasonal variations. The model outputs were calculated in total energy demand (MJ) per day and then summed for a monthly and annual total. The annual energy demand to crop yield (MJ kg-1) or energy use efficiency in each CEA system was then calculated per grid cell. Both monthly energy demand and annual energy use efficiency were downscaled to a 1km grid in order to compare to the higher resolution land use and solar PV potential model outputs. The resulting energy use efficiency as MJ kg-1 for each crop calculated by region for both CEA systems is shown in Fig. 2.

 

Global crop area, yield, and production

We used a data harmonisation approach based on the HILDA+ land use reconstruction model[2], to allocate 2020 crop production (t km-2) and crop harvest area (ha km-2) for the target crops to a 1km global grid array. This approach allowed us to harmonise the outputs of multiple crop models, datasets, and statistical inventories to produce crop area, yield, and production maps for each target crop. In HILDA+, the cropland areas were isolated and used to mask the CROPGRIDS crop-specific crop area data (reference year 2020)[36]. GAEZ v4 (reference year 2015)[35], along with the statistical data for FAO country level harvest area and production quantity totals (reference year 2020)[50] were used to assign the pixel-level harvest area (ha) and yields (t/ha) for the target crops. 

This was done by first normalizing the GAEZ v4 crop yield values, i.e. dividing them by their national and cropland-wide mean, as well as normalizing the CROPGRIDS crop area values by their national and cropland-wide sum (all constrained by HILDA+ cropland and at least 5% CROPGRIDS crop coverage). This normalization was done in order to align each input dataset with the same consistent spatial array and projection. The normalized values, crop yield and area, were then multiplied by FAO crop yield and harvested area in 2020, respectively. The crop production (t) was finally derived by a pixel-based multiplication of country- and crop-specific yield (t ha-1) and harvested areas (ha). Each crop then had a specific harvest area (ha), yield (t ha-1), and production (t) per grid cell for the year 2020. In order to harmonise these different datasets, steps were taken to minimise inter-dataset variability. FAO statistics only report crop area harvested, which could include multiple harvests on the same area, so the CROPGRIDS crop cultivation area layer was used to set a fraction of crop area per grid cell prior to allocating the FAO area harvested within each country’s grid cells. Upper thresholds for crop area were set to limit any instance where the area from multiple harvests were applied to the same grid cell. In this way we were able to remove inconsistencies or data artifacts that would otherwise inflate the crop area beyond what was available in the grid cell (i.e., more than 100 ha crop area for a 100 ha grid cell). The data harmonisation process of crop area, yield, and production is simplified in Supplementary Fig. 4.

 

PV-powered CEA comparison with 2020 crop area, yield, and production

The CEA crop yields[24] were kept constant across the global array in order to test the area and PV energy capacity to scale these experimental values globally. The multiple datasets[35,36,50] used across the analysis reported the reference yields and production in harvested biomass. For this reason, we used CEA production and yield values for harvested biomass. For different research questions, this metric could be changed to dry harvest weight, calories, or other specific nutritional or agronomic units. The first step to calculate the comparison against 2020 crop production was to determine the CEA building area needed to meet 2020 production (t km-2) per grid cell. The annual CEA yields were calculated per growing area and were set per grid cell to reflect the CEA systems (0.75ha growing area per 1ha GH building area and 0.75ha growing area per 0.25ha VF building area). The 2020 production array was divided by the annual CEA yield (per growing area) per crop to give the CEA building area needed for year-round CEA production in each grid cell. This CEA footprint requirement was summed per hectare for GH or per 0.25 hectare for VF per grid cell.

To calculate the solar PV area needed for the CEA, the monthly solar PV potential (kWh m-2) was derived from Saxena et al.[33]. The area available for PV per grid cell was calculated as the harvest area subtracted by the CEA building area per grid cell. The surface area coverage of the solar PV was assumed to be 75% of a given area[22], so the potential energy available to the CEA was reduced by this factor. This PV potential was then multiplied by an efficiency factor[51] (26.8%) for conversion to usable electricity. The total CEA energy demand per building (1ha for GH and 0.25ha for VF) per grid cell was multiplied by the CEA building area requirement to calculate the total CEA energy demand per grid cell. The monthly PV area requirement to directly power the CEA was calculated by multiplying the potential PV energy by the CEA energy demand per grid cell. The process is summarized visually in Supplementary Fig. 3 and all CEA component inputs are summarized in Supplementary Tables 1-4.

For year-round production, the month with the greatest PV area requirement for each grid cell became the fixed PV area needed to power the required CEA area for that grid cell. No energy storage was assumed from one day to the next, so each day had only the monthly 1-day average to fulfil the CEA demand. We also analysed continuous 9-month CEA production capacity as a way to reduce the energy demand and the required PV area to power the CEA. The reduction in yield capacity was taken into account and the CEA area needed to meet 2020-Production per grid cell was re-calculated. For the shortened 9-month production cycle, the 9-month stretch with the lowest PV area requirements to meet indoor energy demands were calculated per grid cell. Similar to the year-round production, the month with the greatest PV area requirement for this 9-month cycle, determined the PV area needed for that grid cell. The resulting area (ha) of PV needed to power a year-round or 9-month CEA is displayed spatially in Supplementary Fig. 7.

This CEA building area plus PV area was the total area that was then compared to the crop harvest area per grid cell. The land area requirement balance (ha) was calculated by subtracting the CEA building footprint plus PV area from the crop area per grid cell. If the area balance was negative, then not enough area was available for the CEA-PV to meet 2020 production in that grid cell. If the balance was zero or positive, the CEA-PV matched 2020 production and any positive value could be considered a lower required land area than 2020 production area in ha. 

Only the grid cells with a positive area balance were used to calculate the potential extra or surplus production by allowing the model to utilise all crop area available and CEA production above 2020 production values. This extra-production was calculated by incrementally adding CEA units (1ha for GH and 0.25ha for VF) and the required PV area per building. This process was done iteratively until the crop harvest area in that grid cell reached zero. The sum of this extra production according to the CEA building area added, was then added to that grid cell total production quantity. The spatial distribution of areas where CEA met 2020 production can be seen in Fig. 3. The global totals and comparison between CEA systems for harvest area (ha) where CEA met 2020 production, production quantity (t) met by CEA, lower CEA-PV land area requirements compared to 2020 production (ha), and extra production (t) by CEA are given in Fig. 4. The regional breakdowns relative to the global totals as well as the breakdown within each region are given in Supplementary Figs. 8&9.

 

Yield gap analysis

The yield gap analysis and comparison were done to apply a single metric for comparing crop production challenges globally. For this study we used the GAEZ v4 crop-wise Yield Achievement Ratio[35] (YAR) global gridded (5 arc minutes) dataset for the most recent average (2009-2011). The YAR was calculated by GAEZ as the ratio of actual (average) yields to the attainable yields for each grid cell. The attainable yields were calculated as the biophysical influences (e.g., solar radiation, water, nutrients, temperature) on yield (potential yield) while considering location specific constraints (e.g., soil or terrain, pest pressure, management). For the crops analysed in this study, GAEZ only has YAR data for wheat, soybean, and potato, so we limited the yield gap analysis to these crops. The ratio of actual/ attainable yields is inversely proportional to the yield gap, as a higher ratio indicates a smaller yield gap. 

We used the GAEZ YAR data that had already been divided into bins corresponding to the crop-wise YAR. The 2020 crop-wise harvest area (ha) was compared to the corresponding YAR to calculate the distribution of crop harvest area per YAR bin. This distribution (percent of harvest area (ha)) per YAR bin was plotted to complement the global YAR maps plotted directly from the GAEZ dataset.

CEA-PV system performance compared to 2020 production was then evaluated against the reference crop yield gaps. Only grid cells where there was spatial agreement between the CROPGRIDS and GAEZ YAR datasets were considered. To analyse CEA-PV relationships with crop yield gaps, only the grid cells where CEA-PV demonstrated the ability to meet 2020 production were considered. Including only these CEA-PV net area positive areas was done to focus on the technical potential of CEA in alleviating yield gap constraints. In our analysis, CEA-PV net negative could not meet the same production values as 2020 production without additional crop area, it was assumed that CEA in these areas would be able to aid in yield gap closures. The area (ha) that was net positive CEA-PV crop area was summed for each YAR bin and the percent of the net positive CEA-PV crop area was plotted alongside the total crop harvest area distribution. Supplementary Fig. 1 provides a general overview of the yield gap analysis process.

 

Electricity grid constraints

The Arderne et al.[52] electrical grid dataset was used to evaluate the current electrical grid coverage in areas that overlap with areas that meet 2020 production (CEA-PV technical capacity areas). Where there was at least medium-voltage electricity, a 2km buffer was set as the maximum distance for connection to these electricity grids. The grid cells where there was overlap of this grid network and buffer with these CEA-PV grid cells that met 2020 production were summed, as well as those that were outside of this 2km buffer. The grid cells were then multiplied by the crop harvest area (ha) in that grid cell and then summed crop at the country- and regional-levels. The proportion of harvest area (ha) where CEA met 2020 production within the 2km electricity grid was then calculated for country and region as seen in Fig. 5. The spatial overlap of areas where CEA met 2020 production and the electricity grid can be seen in Supplementary Fig. 10.

 

Aridity Index

The Global Aridity Index Database as described in Zomer et al.(52) was used to compare where CEA matched 2020 production against aridity zones. The aridity index was divided into bins according to the index value. These index values were overlaid on the grid cells where CEA matched 2020 production. The harvest area (ha) was then multiplied by the number of grid cells within each index bin. The harvest area (ha) where CEA matched 2020 production was plotted according to the aridity index bin and results are given in Supplementary Fig. 11.

 

Model assumption sensitivity

            A deterministic sensitivity analysis was conducted to evaluate CEA-PV equivalent capacity reactions to changes in model assumptions. The sensitivity analysis evaluated changing assumptions around three parameters directly influencing CEA-PV area requirements and subsequent equivalent-capacity calculations: CEA crop yield, CEA energy demand, and PV conversion efficiency. Changes to each assumption were considered individually and for their combined effects on CEA-PV equivalent capacity. The main “baseline” analysis for GH and VF applied the experimental CEA yields described above and calculated the CEA building area required to match 2020 crop production in each grid cell, while the PV area requirement was determined from the corresponding CEA energy demand and a baseline PV conversion efficiency of 26.8%.

For the yield sensitivity analysis, the annual CEA yield for each crop was reduced by 10%, 25%, and 50%. The required CEA building area was then recalculated directly from 2020 crop production using the reduced yield while retaining the same GH- or VF-specific growing areas and corresponding year-round or 9-month growing cycles. The greater CEA area required under lower yields also increased growing area and associated PV area requirements to match 2020 crop production. For the energy sensitivity, CEA energy demand per unit growing area was increased by 10%, 25%, and 50%, while CEA yields and building area requirements were maintained at baseline input values. In turn, the corresponding PV area requirement increased to meet the increased energy demand. For the PV efficiency sensitivity, conversion efficiency was reduced from the baseline input value of 26.8% to 22%, while CEA crop yields and energy demands were kept constant. The PV area requirements were then required to provide the same amount of energy to meet CEA energy demands.

Additionally, the joint effects of combining CEA yield reductions, energy demand increases, and PV conversion efficiency reductions were evaluated. For each joint effect scenario, the revised CEA building area and PV requirements were compared to the available crop-wise harvested area in each grid cell using the same approach as the baseline analysis to calculate equivalent capacity. The sensitivity analysis tested the change in absolute area (ha), production (t), and less crop area required (ha) and corresponding global percentages for the CEA systems, year-round and 9-month growing cycles, and four crops. The sensitivity analysis therefore tested how these CEA systems performed under less favourable model assumptions rather than representing probabilistic uncertainty ranges.

descriptions.description:
Marine heatwaves (MHWs) are devastating extreme ocean temperature events
 whose frequency and severity have surged under global warming, threatening
 marine ecosystems and fisheries. Yet the fundamental mechanisms that
 control their intensity and persistence remain incompletely understood.
 Here, using a submesoscale-permitting global model simulation validated by
 long-term observational and reanalysis data, this study reveals a
 previously overlooked submesoscale feedback that exerts a critical control
 on MHW severity. It is demonstrated that the submesoscale-induced vertical
 heat flux suppresses the intensity and persistence of atmospheric-driven
 MHWs in winter via a negative feedback mechanism. Enhanced air-sea net
 heat flux strengthens stratification and shallows the mixed layer,
 weakening submesoscale vertical heat transport by 19.4%, reducing MHW
 intensification by 18.1%, and accelerating decay by 21.7%. This missing
 regulatory mechanism indicates that models ignoring submesoscales likely
 overestimate MHW severity, with critical implications for future climate
 projections.

# Submesoscale Feedback Suppresses Marine Heatwaves: data and code for
 figures [Access this dataset on
 Dryad](https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.hdr7sqw02) ## Summary This dataset
 contains the processed numerical data and MATLAB plotting scripts used to
 reproduce Figures 1–4 and Supplementary Figures S1–S4 for the study
 **“Submesoscale Feedback Suppresses Marine Heatwaves.”** The files
 include: * marine heatwave (MHW) event statistics derived from the LLC4320
 simulation and NOAA OISST v2.1; * phase-averaged upper-ocean MHW
 heat-budget terms from LLC4320; * statistics for four MHW driver types; *
 submesoscale heat-flux, activity, and mixed-layer-depth diagnostics; and *
 GLORYS12V1-based parameterized submesoscale vertical heat-flux
 diagnostics. The repository contains **processed data used for the
 figures**, not the full raw LLC4320, OISST, or GLORYS12V1 source datasets.
 Links to those source datasets are provided below. There are paired files
 for each reproduced figure: `FigN.mat` contains the processed data and
 `FigN.m` is the MATLAB script that reads that file and creates the
 corresponding figure. Files beginning with `FigS` correspond to
 Supplementary Figures. **Figure 5 is a conceptual schematic and therefore
 has no numerical data file in this repository.** ## Terminology and common
 conventions * **MHW**: marine heatwave. * **LLC4320**: the nominal 1/48°
 global MITgcm simulation used for the high-resolution analysis. *
 **OISST**: NOAA Optimum Interpolation Sea Surface Temperature v2.1, 0.25°
 daily SST. * **GLORYS12V1**: Copernicus Marine global ocean reanalysis at
 1/12° horizontal resolution. * **Onset / grow phase**: the period from MHW
 onset to the time of maximum spatially integrated temperature anomaly. *
 **Decay phase**: the period from that maximum to the end of the MHW. *
 **T_Tendency**: tendency of the horizontally integrated upper-50-m
 temperature anomaly. * **T_Qnet**: contribution from anomalous net surface
 heat flux. * **T_BF**: heat-budget contribution associated with the
 background current field. * **T_SF**: heat-budget contribution associated
 with submesoscale currents. * **T_SVF**: vertical heat-flux contribution
 driven by submesoscale perturbations. * **T_MSVF**: mean/background
 submesoscale vertical heat flux, obtained from the 60-day moving-average
 fields. * **BF&BF**: T_BF is the dominant driver during both onset and
 decay. * **BF&Qnet**: T_BF dominates onset and T_Qnet dominates decay.
 * **Qnet&BF**: T_Qnet dominates onset and T_BF dominates decay. *
 **Qnet&Qnet**: T_Qnet is the dominant driver during both onset and
 decay. * **Qnet-dominated MHWs**: the Qnet&BF and Qnet&Qnet types
 combined. Unless otherwise stated, longitude is in degrees east on a
 0–360° grid and latitude is in degrees north (negative values indicate the
 Southern Hemisphere). ### Sign convention in the saved heat-budget arrays
 Some `.mat` files retain the internal sign convention used during the
 budget calculation. The supplied plotting scripts apply the sign changes
 used in the published figures. In particular: * `Fig2.m` plots
 `-Qnet_*_grid`, `-mean_*_grid`, and `-sub_*_grid`, while `dTdt_*_grid` is
 plotted without a sign change. * `Fig3.m` similarly plots `-Qnet_*`,
 `-mean_*`, and `-sub_*` from the structures in `Fig3.mat`. * `Fig4.m`
 plots `-sub_tot`, `-sub_vert`, and `-sub_vert_mean`. * `FigS4.m` plots the
 variables in `FigS4.mat` without this additional sign reversal. Users
 wishing to reproduce the published panels should therefore use the paired
 `.m` scripts rather than applying an independent sign convention. ## File
 naming and file structure The repository contains the following research
 files: * `Fig1.m`, `Fig1.mat` — data and plotting code for main Figure 1.
 * `Fig2.m`, `Fig2.mat` — data and plotting code for main Figure 2. *
 `Fig3.m`, `Fig3.mat` — data and plotting code for main Figure 3. *
 `Fig4.m`, `Fig4.mat` — data and plotting code for main Figure 4. *
 `FigS1.m`, `FigS1.mat` — data and plotting code for Supplementary Figure
 S1. * `FigS2.m`, `FigS2.mat` — data and plotting code for Supplementary
 Figure S2. * `FigS3.m`, `FigS3.mat` — data and plotting code for
 Supplementary Figure S3. * `FigS4.m`, `FigS4.mat` — data and plotting code
 for Supplementary Figure S4. `FigS1.mat` is stored in MATLAB v7.3/HDF5
 format. The other `.mat` files use the standard MATLAB MAT-file format. No
 special numeric missing-value code such as `-9999` is used. Where present,
 `NaN` denotes a missing/unavailable grid value. In padded event-by-time
 arrays in `Fig1.mat`, only the first `dur_time(i)` columns for event `i`
 should be interpreted as valid event days. --- ## Main Figure 1 —
 `Fig1.mat` and `Fig1.m` ### Purpose Figure 1 compares wintertime MHW
 counts and space-time integrated MHW intensity from LLC4320 and OISST,
 both globally and in selected subregions. The regional abbreviations are:
 * `glb`: global ocean; * `cnp`: Central North Pacific (CNP); * `gulf`:
 Gulf Stream (GS); * `iso`: Indian Ocean sector of the Southern Ocean
 (ISO); * `pso`: Pacific Ocean sector of the Southern Ocean (PSO); * `bcs`:
 Brazil Current System (BCS). ### Top-level variables in `Fig1.mat` * `xx0`
 (18 × 36): longitude coordinates for the 10° × 10° plotting grid, degrees
 east. * `yy0` (18 × 36): latitude coordinates for the 10° × 10° plotting
 grid, degrees north. * `mhw_llc`: structure containing LLC4320 event-level
 and gridded MHW information. * `mhw_oisst`: structure containing the
 corresponding OISST information. * `glb`, `cnp`, `gulf`, `iso`, `pso`,
 `bcs`: regional summary structures. ### Fields in `mhw_llc` and
 `mhw_oisst` The two structures use the same field names. * `x` (720 ×
 1440): longitude-column index matrix for the underlying 0.25° grid;
 integer index, no physical unit. * `y` (720 × 1440): latitude-row index
 matrix for the underlying 0.25° grid; integer index, no physical unit. *
 `mhw_event1` (event × time cell array): for each event day, an `N × 2`
 list of `[row_index, column_index]` grid cells belonging to that spatial
 MHW event. Cells after the event duration are padding/unused. *
 `temp_area_event1` (event × time): daily SST anomaly integrated over the
 event area, °C km². * `temp_mean_event1` (event × time): daily
 spatial-mean SST anomaly over the event area, °C. * `area_event1` (event ×
 time): daily MHW area, km². * `dur_time` (event): event duration, days. *
 `temp_area_mean` (event): sum of `temp_area_event1` over the valid event
 days; this is the space-time integrated event intensity, °C km² days. *
 `temp_mean_mean` (event): sum of `temp_mean_event1` over the valid event
 days, °C days. * `area_mean` (event): sum of `area_event1` over the valid
 event days, km² days. * `loc_event` (event × 2): representative event
 location `[longitude, latitude]`, defined from the event geometry and used
 for spatial binning; degrees east and degrees north. * `dur_grid` (18 ×
 36): gridded accumulated event-duration diagnostic, days. * `num_grid` (18
 × 36): number of spatial MHW events assigned to each 10° × 10° grid box,
 count. * `intense_grid` (18 × 36): gridded accumulated time-integrated
 spatial-mean MHW intensity, °C days. * `area_grid` (18 × 36): gridded
 accumulated area-time diagnostic, km² days. * `intense_area_grid` (18 ×
 36): gridded cumulative space-time integrated SST anomaly used for the
 MHW-intensity maps, °C km² days. ### Fields in the regional summary
 structures Each of `glb`, `cnp`, `gulf`, `iso`, `pso`, and `bcs` contains:
 * `num_mhw_llc`: number of LLC4320 spatial MHW events in that region,
 count. * `intense_mhw_llc`: total LLC4320 space-time integrated MHW
 intensity in that region, °C km² days. * `num_mhw_oisst`: number of OISST
 spatial MHW events in that region, count. * `intense_mhw_oisst`: total
 OISST space-time integrated MHW intensity in that region, °C km² days.
 `Fig1.m` reads these variables and exports `Fig1.pdf`. --- ## Main Figure
 2 — `Fig2.mat` and `Fig2.m` ### Purpose Figure 2 shows the global spatial
 distributions of the phase-averaged upper-50-m MHW heat-budget terms
 during the onset and decay phases. ### Variables in `Fig2.mat` All
 heat-budget arrays are 36 × 18 and are stored as longitude × latitude.
 Their physical unit before the plotting factor of `1e3` is °C km² s⁻¹. *
 `xx0` (36): longitude centers of the 10° × 10° grid, degrees east. * `yy0`
 (18): latitude centers of the 10° × 10° grid, degrees north. *
 `dTdt_grow_grid`: phase-averaged T_Tendency during MHW onset, °C km² s⁻¹.
 * `dTdt_decay_grid`: phase-averaged T_Tendency during MHW decay, °C km²
 s⁻¹. * `Qnet_grow_grid`: saved net-surface-heat-flux budget term during
 onset, °C km² s⁻¹; `Fig2.m` multiplies this field by `-1` for the plotted
 T_Qnet convention. * `Qnet_decay_grid`: corresponding decay-phase field;
 same units and sign treatment. * `mean_grow_grid`: saved
 background-current budget term during onset, °C km² s⁻¹; plotted as T_BF
 after multiplication by `-1`. * `mean_decay_grid`: corresponding
 decay-phase field; same units and sign treatment. * `sub_grow_grid`: saved
 submesoscale-current budget term during onset, °C km² s⁻¹; plotted as T_SF
 after multiplication by `-1`. * `sub_decay_grid`: corresponding
 decay-phase field; same units and sign treatment. `grow` in the variable
 name means the onset/intensification phase. `decay` means the decay phase.
 `Fig2.m` transposes the 36 × 18 data arrays for map plotting and exports
 `Fig2.pdf`. --- ## Main Figure 3 — `Fig3.mat` and `Fig3.m` ### Purpose
 Figure 3 compares the globally averaged MHW heat-budget terms for four
 objectively classified MHW types and for the onset and decay phases. Error
 bars are 95% confidence intervals estimated from event-based samples using
 5000 bootstrap resamples. ### Top-level structures and MHW-type mapping *
 `mhw_mean_mean` → BF&BF. * `mhw_mean_Qnet` → BF&Qnet. *
 `mhw_Qnet_mean` → Qnet&BF. * `mhw_Qnet_Qnet` → Qnet&Qnet. The word
 `mean` in these structure names refers to the background-flow/BF branch
 used in the original analysis naming; it should not be interpreted as a
 generic arithmetic mean. ### Fields in each structure All central
 estimates have units of °C km² s⁻¹. Each field ending in `_ci` is a
 two-element vector `[lower, upper]` giving the bootstrap 95% confidence
 interval in the same units and in the same saved sign convention as its
 corresponding estimate. * `dTdt_grow`, `dTdt_grow_ci`: onset-phase
 T_Tendency and 95% CI. * `dTdt_decay`, `dTdt_decay_ci`: decay-phase
 T_Tendency and 95% CI. * `Qnet_grow`, `Qnet_grow_ci`: saved onset-phase
 surface-heat-flux term. `Fig3.m` multiplies it by `-1` to obtain the
 plotted T_Qnet. * `Qnet_decay`, `Qnet_decay_ci`: decay-phase equivalent. *
 `mean_grow`, `mean_grow_ci`: saved onset-phase background-current term.
 `Fig3.m` multiplies it by `-1` to obtain the plotted T_BF. * `mean_decay`,
 `mean_decay_ci`: decay-phase equivalent. * `sub_grow`, `sub_grow_ci`:
 saved onset-phase submesoscale term. `Fig3.m` multiplies it by `-1` to
 obtain the plotted T_SF. * `sub_decay`, `sub_decay_ci`: decay-phase
 equivalent. * `wt_grow`, `wt_grow_ci`: auxiliary onset-phase submesoscale
 vertical heat-flux diagnostic associated with the vertical
 `w'T'` contribution (T_SVF); this field is retained in the data
 file but is not used directly by `Fig3.m`. * `wt_decay`, `wt_decay_ci`:
 corresponding decay-phase vertical heat-flux diagnostic; also not used
 directly by `Fig3.m`. The residual shown in Figure 3 is not stored as a
 separate variable. It is calculated in `Fig3.m` from T_Tendency minus the
 sum of the displayed T_Qnet, T_BF, and T_SF terms. `Fig3.m` exports
 `Fig3.pdf`. --- ## Main Figure 4 — `Fig4.mat` and `Fig4.m` ### Purpose
 Figure 4 shows the spatial distributions of submesoscale heat-flux terms
 during Qnet-dominated MHWs. ### Variables in `Fig4.mat` The 36 × 18 fields
 are stored as longitude × latitude. Units are °C km² s⁻¹ before the
 plotting factor of `1e3`. * `xx0` (36): longitude centers of the 10° × 10°
 grid, degrees east. * `yy0` (18): latitude centers of the 10° × 10° grid,
 degrees north. * `sub_tot` (36 × 18): total submesoscale heat-budget
 contribution corresponding to T_SF, °C km² s⁻¹. * `sub_vert` (36 × 18):
 submesoscale vertical heat-flux contribution corresponding to T_SVF, °C
 km² s⁻¹. * `sub_vert_mean` (36 × 18): mean/background submesoscale
 vertical heat flux corresponding to T_MSVF, °C km² s⁻¹. `Fig4.m`
 multiplies all three heat-flux arrays by `-1` before plotting and exports
 `Fig4.pdf`. --- ## Supplementary Figure S1 — `FigS1.mat` and `FigS1.m` ###
 Purpose Figure S1 compares MHWs detected in OISST and LLC4320 at the
 example location 175.875°W, 31.375°N over 15 October 2011–15 October 2012.
 `FigS1.mat` is a MATLAB v7.3/HDF5 file. ### Variables in `FigS1.mat` *
 `time` (367): daily time coordinate stored as MATLAB serial date numbers;
 spans 2011-10-15 through 2012-10-15. * `temp_oisst` (367): daily OISST SST
 at the example grid point, °C. * `temp_llc` (367): daily LLC4320 SST at
 the example grid point, °C. * `mclim_oisst` (366): day-of-year
 climatological SST used for OISST MHW detection, °C. * `mclim_llc` (366):
 day-of-year climatological SST used for LLC4320 MHW detection, °C. In this
 file the observational climatology is used as the reference for the model
 detection. * `m90_oisst` (366): day-of-year 90th-percentile SST threshold,
 °C. * `m90_llc` (366): day-of-year 90th-percentile SST threshold used for
 LLC4320, °C. * `MHW_oisst` (9 events × 9 columns): OISST MHW event table.
 * `MHW_llc` (8 events × 9 columns): LLC4320 MHW event table. ### Column
 definitions for `MHW_oisst` and `MHW_llc` 1. start date, integer
 `YYYYMMDD`; 2. end date, integer `YYYYMMDD`; 3. duration, days; 4. maximum
 MHW intensity relative to the climatology, °C; 5. mean MHW intensity
 relative to the climatology, °C; 6. within-event intensity variability
 (standard deviation), °C; 7. cumulative MHW intensity, °C days; 8.
 longitude-grid index for the selected location, integer index; 9.
 latitude-grid index for the selected location, integer index. `FigS1.m`
 uses these data to shade detected MHW periods and exports `FigS1.pdf`. ---
 ## Supplementary Figure S2 — `FigS2.mat` and `FigS2.m` ### Purpose Figure
 S2 compares grid-point MHW statistics between LLC4320 and OISST, including
 event counts, duration, mean intensity, and cumulative intensity. These
 are grid-point MHW statistics and therefore the event counts are not the
 same quantity as the spatially connected event counts in Figure 1. ###
 Coordinates * `lon` (1440): longitude of the 0.25° grid, degrees east. *
 `lat` (720): latitude of the 0.25° grid, degrees north. ### Spatial
 structures `llc_spatial` and `oisst_spatial` each contain 1440 × 720
 longitude × latitude arrays: * `num`: number of detected grid-point MHW
 events, count. * `dur`: average MHW duration at the grid point, days. *
 `int_max`: average maximum MHW intensity, °C. * `int_mean`: average mean
 MHW intensity, °C. * `int_var`: average MHW intensity variability, °C. *
 `int_cum`: average cumulative MHW intensity, °C days. `NaN` values in
 these spatial metrics indicate locations without an available metric (for
 example, where no qualifying MHW statistic is present). ### Regional
 summary structures The file contains paired summary structures for LLC4320
 and OISST: * `glb_llc`, `glb_oisst` — global; * `cnp_llc`, `cnp_oisst` —
 Central North Pacific; * `gulf_llc`, `gulf_oisst` — Gulf Stream; *
 `iso_llc`, `iso_oisst` — Indian Ocean sector of the Southern Ocean; *
 `pso_llc`, `pso_oisst` — Pacific Ocean sector of the Southern Ocean; *
 `bcs_llc`, `bcs_oisst` — Brazil Current System. Each regional structure
 contains: * `num`: total grid-point MHW count in the region, count. *
 `dur`: regional mean MHW duration, days. * `dur_std`: standard deviation
 associated with duration, days. * `int_mean`: regional mean MHW mean
 intensity, °C. * `int_mean_std`: standard deviation associated with mean
 intensity, °C. * `int_cum`: regional mean cumulative MHW intensity, °C
 days. * `int_cum_std`: standard deviation associated with cumulative
 intensity, °C days. `FigS2.m` exports `FigS2.pdf`. --- ## Supplementary
 Figure S3 — `FigS3.mat` and `FigS3.m` ### Purpose Figure S3 shows
 integrated submesoscale activity and mixed-layer-depth (MLD) diagnostics
 during Qnet-dominated MHWs. Submesoscale activity is characterized in the
 analysis by the standard deviation of normalized vertical relative
 vorticity (`ζ/f`) within a 0.25° × 0.25° neighborhood. The anomaly fields
 are obtained relative to the corresponding 60-day moving-average
 background before integration over the MHW area. ### Variables in
 `FigS3.mat` * `lon4` (36): longitude centers of the 10° × 10° composite
 grid, degrees east. * `lat4` (18): latitude centers of the 10° × 10°
 composite grid, degrees north. * `ro_an` (18 × 36, latitude × longitude):
 integrated submesoscale-activity anomaly during MHWs, km². The plotted
 figure divides this value by `1e3` and labels the scale as ×10³ km². *
 `rom` (18 × 36): integrated mean/background submesoscale activity, km².
 The plotted figure divides by `1e3`. * `mld_an` (18 × 36): integrated
 mixed-layer-depth anomaly during MHWs, m km². The plotted figure
 multiplies by `1e-5` and labels the scale as ×10⁵ m km². * `mldm` (18 ×
 36): integrated mean/background mixed-layer depth, m km². The plotted
 figure multiplies by `1e-5`. The mixed-layer depth is defined as the depth
 at which the density differs by 0.03 kg m⁻³ from the value at 10 m depth.
 `FigS3.m` exports `FigS3.pdf`. --- ## Supplementary Figure S4 —
 `FigS4.mat` and `FigS4.m` ### Purpose Figure S4 contains the
 GLORYS12V1-based estimate of submesoscale-induced vertical heat flux
 during MHWs using the Fox-Kemper et al. mixed-layer eddy parameterization,
 including sensitivity calculations that isolate the influence of
 mixed-layer depth and horizontal buoyancy/temperature gradients. ###
 Variables in `FigS4.mat` The 36 × 18 fields are stored as longitude ×
 latitude. Units are °C km² s⁻¹ before the plotting factor of `1e3`. *
 `xx0` (36): longitude centers of the 10° × 10° grid, degrees east. * `yy0`
 (18): latitude centers of the 10° × 10° grid, degrees north. * `subflx`
 (36 × 18): MHW-related submesoscale vertical heat-flux anomaly, T_SVF,
 after removal of the mean/background flux, °C km² s⁻¹. * `subflx_mean` (36
 × 18): mean/background submesoscale vertical heat flux, T_MSVF, °C km²
 s⁻¹. * `subflx_mld` (36 × 18): vertical heat-flux change associated with
 MLD variability while horizontal buoyancy and temperature gradients are
 replaced by their 60-day moving averages, °C km² s⁻¹. * `subflx_bgrd` (36
 × 18): vertical heat-flux change associated with buoyancy- and
 temperature-gradient variability while MLD is replaced by its 60-day
 moving average, °C km² s⁻¹. A small number of cells contain `NaN`; these
 should be treated as missing/unavailable values. `FigS4.m` exports
 `FigS4.pdf`. --- ## Sharing/Access information ### Raw/source datasets
 from which the processed files were derived * **LLC4320 / ECCO simulation
 output:**
 [https://data.nas.nasa.gov/ecco/data.php](https://data.nas.nasa.gov/ecco/data.php)\ The data can also be accessed using the `xmitgcm` package: [https://xmitgcm.readthedocs.io/en/latest/index.html](https://xmitgcm.readthedocs.io/en/latest/index.html) * **NOAA OISST v2.1:** [https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/data/sea-surface-temperature-optimum-interpolation/v2.1/access/avhrr/](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/data/sea-surface-temperature-optimum-interpolation/v2.1/access/avhrr/) * **GLORYS12V1 / Copernicus Marine Service:** [https://doi.org/10.48670/moi-00021](https://doi.org/10.48670/moi-00021) The present Dryad deposit contains only the processed values needed for the figure-level analyses and does not redistribute the complete source datasets listed above. ## Code/Software All plotting scripts are written in MATLAB. The exact MATLAB release used to create the archived files is not encoded in the submitted files. The scripts use `exportgraphics`, so a MATLAB release supporting that function is needed for unchanged execution. ### Required or referenced MATLAB functionality * Standard MATLAB plotting and MAT-file functions. * **M_Map** mapping toolbox for functions such as `m_proj`, `m_contourf`, `m_pcolor`, `m_plot`, `m_coast`, `m_grid`, and `m_text`. * **cptcmap** for GMT-style color maps. * **cmocean** for the `matter` color map used in `Fig1.m`. * `FigS1.m` also uses `internal.stats.parseArgs` and `internal.stats.getParamVal` in its plotting setup; these are MATLAB internal Statistics functions in installations where they are available. ### Important note for `FigS1.m` `FigS1.m` calls a local helper function named `datemon` to generate date tick positions. titles.title: Dataset of ground-based meteorological observations and sunshine duration for solar irradiance modelling in Central Java, Indonesia

descriptions.description:
This dataset provides three years (1 January 2022 - 31 December 2024) of daily ground-based meteorological observations from the Sempu climatological station in Central Java, Indonesia (7.411 S, 110.237 E), together with a co-located NASA POWER daily time series retrieved for the same coordinates and period, and a quality-controlled, analysis-ready file merging the two sources.

The ground-based observations are distributed by the Central Java Provincial Public Works Agency for Water Resources and Spatial Planning (Dinas PUSDATARU). They comprise daily mean air temperature, relative humidity, wind speed, and sunshine duration (as a percentage of the maximum possible duration). The NASA POWER series provides all-sky surface shortwave downward irradiance (global horizontal irradiance, GHI) and ancillary 2 m meteorology.

Long, openly licensed, station-level daily records from the Indonesian maritime continent are scarce. By pairing measured sunshine duration with a co-located satellite/reanalysis series on a common daily time base, the dataset supports developing and evaluating sunshine-based empirical estimates of daily GHI under humid tropical conditions, benchmarking machine-learning irradiance models, and cross-comparing ground meteorology against reanalysis. It also suits reference-evapotranspiration, agro-climatic, and renewable-energy resource assessment.

Notes for reuse. (1) GHI is a NASA POWER satellite-derived product, not a ground pyranometer measurement; the station has no pyranometer. The data support estimating GHI from ground meteorology, not validating satellite irradiance against an independent ground reference. (2) The source reports daily maximum and minimum temperature, but on about 82% of days the daily range is exactly 1.0 C and the mean is their exact midpoint, indicating the extremes are derived from the mean rather than measured. They are kept only in the raw file for transparency and excluded from the analysis-ready file, which retains the daily mean temperature (Tavg).

Files. (a) sempu_klimatologi_2022_2024.xlsx - raw observations, 1,096 records (date, RH, Tmax, Tmin, Tavg, WS, Sunshine_%). (b) Data_power_nasa_sempu.xlsx - NASA POWER, 1,096 records (Date, GHI, T2M, RH2M, WS2M). (c) master_dataset_irradiance_sempu.csv - analysis-ready, 1,056 records (date, Tavg, RH, WS, Sunshine_%, GHI). (d) qc_merge_sempu.py - script reproducing (c). (e) README.txt - documentation.

Units: Tavg C; RH %; WS km/h; Sunshine_% %; GHI kWh/m2/day. Dates local time (WIB, UTC+7), ISO 8601; point decimal separator; empty cells = missing.
