titles.title: Emerging compound air-soil heatwaves amplify global vegetation losses

affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)
creators.name: Liu, Zhen

affiliation: Institute of Geographic Sciences and Natural Resources Research, Chinese Academy of Sciences
creators.name: Pei, Tao

descriptions.description:
Emerging compound air-soil heatwaves amplify global vegetation losses 

 

This repository contains the Python code and processed data used to reproduce the main figures and analyses of independent air heatwaves, independent soil heatwaves, and compound air-soil heatwaves. The original ERA5, MERRA-2, CMIP6, and GPP datasets are not included because of their large file sizes. Instead, we provide the processed metrics used to reproduce the analyses and figures in the main text.

 

Codes information:

[3-1] Spatial characteristicsPlots the spatial distributions and regional statistics of heatwave frequency, duration, maximum intensity, and cumulative intensity using the processed reanalysis metrics.

[3-2] Historical temporal changesCalculates and plots the long-term changes in heatwave metrics.

[3-3] Spatial trendsCalculates grid-cell trends using the Theil-Sen estimator and modified Mann-Kendall test and plots their spatial distributions and regional trends.

[4] GPP responsesAnalyzes GPP anomalies associated with the three heatwave types, including event-period responses and GPP changes before and after heatwave events.

[5] Future projectionsAnalyzes historical and future heatwave metrics from CMIP6 simulations and compares projected changes under SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5.

 

 

All data used in this study are publicly available under the following URLs:

l  The ERA5 dataset is available via the Copernicus Climate Data Store (CDS) at https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu/cdsapp#!/dataset/reanalysis-era5-complete?tab=form.

l  The MERRA2 data are available at https://disc.gsfc.nasa.gov/ datasets/M2T1NXSLV_5.12.4/summary.

l  Data for historical simulations (1961–2014) and future projections (2015–2100) of daily near-surface air temperature and daily (or sub-daily) soil temperature are from the sixth phase of the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP6) (https://esgf-node.llnl.gov/search/cmip6/).

l  BESS v2.0 GPP data are download from https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1ZJWSwBDcz9mHU2FXXtUTpAMrjstj1b6n.

l  BEPS GPP model data are download from https://www.nesdc.org.cn/sdo/detail?id=612f42ee7e28172cbed3d809.

l  FluxSat GPP data are download from https://doi.org/10.5067/MEASURES/FLUXSAT/FLUXSATMGPP_L3_DAILY_P5DEG.2.2.

titles.title: Database of global glacier terminus type, dynamics and climate for RGI 6.0 glaciers

descriptions.description:
This database incorporates glacier properties and climate data from multiple sources for the ~216,000 glaciers listed in the Randolph Glacier Inventory (RGI) v.6.0, alongside a new globally-complete classification of glacier terminus types distinguishing between land, lake, marine and shelf environments. The database was compiled to quantify associations between terminus type and glacier dynamics (velocity and specific mass change) at the global scale.

The dataset comprises the following measurements for RGI 6.0 glaciers globally: glacier locations and geometric properties from RGI 6.0; mean annual air temperature and total annual precipitation (1991-2020) derived from ECMWF ERA5 reanalysis data; median glacier thickness values (2017-2018) from Millan et al. (2022); median glacier surface velocities (2017-2018) from Millan et al. (2022) and MEaSUREs Greenland surface velocity mosaics; mass change rates (2000-2019) from Hugonnet et al. (2021); supraglacial debris cover extents (2015-2017) from Scherler et al. (2018); glacier proximity to volcano data from Edwards et al. (2020); and glacier terminus type classifications featuring lake classifications newly produced in this study, and land-, marine-, and shelf-terminating classifications retained from RGI 6.0.

This dataset accompanies the paper: Mallalieu et al. (2026) Global-scale variability of glacier velocity and mass loss across terminus environments. Nature Communications. doi: TBC. Full details are provided in the accompanying README file and in the manuscript methods section.

R code to reproduce the analysis and figures presented in the manuscript is available from GitHub.

titles.title: PLI-Parallax: multi-predictor and experimental protein-ligand coordinates with distance and contact labels

descriptions.description:
With structure prediction now accurate enough to serve as training signal, virtual screening input and starting poses for refinement, the volume of available protein-ligand geometry exceeds what experiments have produced. How much of it to trust is usually decided by the confidence score of the model that produced it. Whether that score tracks accuracy, rather than the model's own certainty, can usually not be determined from the prediction alone.

This dataset serves two purposes: it supplies a large corpus of predicted and experimental protein-ligand geometry, and it records how the predictions relate to one another and to experimental data, so that the trust question can be examined on the same data it applies to. It provides three-dimensional coordinates generated by running three structure-prediction and docking programs in four configurations over shared inputs, together with residue-to-ligand-atom distance labels derived from those coordinates. The teachers are Chai-1, Boltz-2 in single-sequence and alignment-conditioned configurations, and smina docking into a predicted receptor.

The corpus tier holds 31,746 non-cognate BindingDB pairs modelled on AlphaFold receptors, where every coordinate is a prediction. The crystal tier holds 19,350 BioLiP2 complexes whose deposited coordinates serve as ground truth. Inter-teacher agreement is measured against a known answer on the crystal tier and calibrated there. On the corpus tier the calibration is applied to systems where no such reference exists.

An HDF5 coordinate store carries (per system and per teacher) the C-alpha position, a side-chain centroid and the backbone carbonyl carbon position for every residue, every receptor heavy atom within 15 Angstrom of the ligand, and ligand coordinates for up to five poses on a five-slot teacher axis with experimental ground truth at index zero. The per-residue arrays are aligned by position, so a C-alpha, two-bead or three-bead view is a column selection. Coordinates are mean-centred per system as int16 at 0.01 Angstrom. Parquet tables materialise the store at the 15 Angstrom cutoff, giving C-alpha and nearest heavy-atom distances and contact flags at 4, 5 and 8 Angstrom, both recomputable from the store.

Also included: 646 leakage-controlled split configurations across seven families with measured shift diagnostics; a teacher-agreement table, median pairwise ligand-centroid separation 18.2 Angstrom on the corpus tier and 11.5 on the crystal tier after superposition; per-system reliability with a split-conformal interval; pocket annotations from three detectors over 20,404 receptors; per-residue support; a field dictionary; Croissant metadata; and a SHA-256 manifest. Multi-method predictions have been deposited before for benchmark sets of a few hundred experimentally solved systems. What this record adds is the corpus tier, where no experimental structure exists and the agreement between teachers carries the signal on its own, together with the calibration that makes it interpretable.

As the store is not all-atom, tools needing full geometry cannot run on it. Contact rows are censored at the cutoff, covering 23.5 per cent of a system's residues on average. Coverage is bounded by a receptor length cap on the cofolding arms and by metal macrocycles that fail conformer generation. Details are in the accompanying Data Descriptor. The deposit ships as a single archive. Extract with tar xf pli_parallax_v1.0.0.tar into an empty directory and verify with sha256sum -c MANIFEST.sha256, which reports 43 files. The README, the Croissant metadata and the manifest are also provided unarchived so the record can be inspected before download.

titles.title: TFBindFormer Dataset v1.1.0

descriptions.description:
This dataset contains the training, validation, and test data used for transcription factor (TF)–DNA binding prediction in the revised TFBindFormer framework. It integrates genomic DNA sequence data, TF protein sequence and structural information, processed TF representations, cell-type metadata, and pre-generated DNA–TF sampling indices to support reproducible model training, evaluation, and zero-shot testing on unseen transcription factors.

DNA Sequence Data (dna_data/)

The dna_data directory contains one-hot-encoded genomic DNA sequence data and corresponding TF-binding labels, organized into three mutually exclusive dataset splits:



train/ – training data



train_data.npy

train_labels.npy



val/ – validation data



val_data.npy

val_labels.npy



test/ – held-out test data



test_data.npy

test_labels.npy




The DNA inputs correspond to genomic sequence windows used by TFBindFormer for TF-binding prediction. The label arrays contain the corresponding TF-binding annotations for each DNA sequence.

The genomic data are partitioned using chromosome-based splits. The training set contains chromosomes other than chr4, chr7, chr8, chr9, and chrY. Chromosomes chr4 and chr7 are used for validation, while chr8 and chr9 are reserved for testing.

Each input sequence represents a 1,000-bp genomic window centered on a 200-bp genomic bin. A TF-binding label is considered positive when at least 50% of the corresponding 200-bp bin overlaps a ChIP-seq narrowPeak region.

Metadata (metadata/)

The metadata directory contains metadata describing the TF–cell-type prediction tasks and the cell-type identifiers used by the model.



seen_tf_metadata.tsv – metadata for TF–cell-type tasks associated with transcription factors represented during model training.

unseen_tf_metadata.tsv – metadata for TF–cell-type tasks associated with transcription factors excluded from training and reserved for zero-shot evaluation.

seen_cell_type_ids.npy – encoded cell-type identifiers corresponding to the seen-TF tasks.

unseen_cell_type_ids.npy – encoded cell-type identifiers corresponding to the unseen-TF tasks.


The metadata files provide mappings among transcription factors, cell types or experimental conditions, and their corresponding prediction tasks.

The revised TFBindFormer dataset contains:



100 seen TFs, corresponding to 422 TF–cell-type tasks

8 unseen TFs, corresponding to 35 TF–cell-type tasks


The unseen TFs are completely excluded from model training and are used exclusively to evaluate zero-shot generalization to previously unseen transcription factors.

Transcription Factor Data (tf_data/)

The tf_data directory contains TF protein sequence, structural, and processed representation data used by the TFBindFormer protein encoder.

Amino-Acid Sequences (aa_sequences/)

The aa_sequences directory contains amino-acid FASTA sequences for all seen and unseen TFs included in the dataset.

These protein sequences provide the sequence information used to generate pretrained TF representations.

Protein Structures (pdb_structures/)

The pdb_structures directory contains protein structure files in PDB format for all seen and unseen TFs.

These structures are used to derive Foldseek 3Di structural representations.

Foldseek 3Di Structural Sequences (foldseek_3Di_ss.fasta)

foldseek_3Di_ss.fasta contains precomputed Foldseek 3Di structural token sequences derived from the TF protein structures.

The 3Di representation converts local three-dimensional protein environments into discrete structural tokens, providing structure-aware information that complements amino-acid sequence information.

ProstT5 Embeddings (prostt5_embeddings/)

The prostt5_embeddings directory contains precomputed TF protein embeddings for the seen and unseen TFs generated using ProstT5-based sequence and structural representations.

These embeddings are stored before conversion to the fixed-length protein representations used directly by TFBindFormer.

Fixed-Length TF Representations (fixed_length_200/)

TF proteins vary in sequence length. Before being provided to the TFBindFormer model, their protein representations are standardized to a fixed length of 200 tokens.

The fixed_length_200 directory contains the final model-ready TF representations and is divided into seen- and unseen-TF sets.

Seen TFs (fixed_length_200/seen_tf/)



fixed_tf_embs.pt

fixed_tf_masks.pt

tf_names_in_label_order.tsv


fixed_tf_embs.pt contains the fixed-length protein embeddings for TFs represented during model training.

fixed_tf_masks.pt contains the corresponding masks used to distinguish valid protein-token positions from padded positions.

tf_names_in_label_order.tsv records the TF ordering corresponding to the protein tensors and TF-binding label ordering. This file ensures that each protein representation is correctly matched to its corresponding prediction task.

Unseen TFs (fixed_length_200/unseen_tf/)



fixed_tf_embs.pt

fixed_tf_masks.pt

tf_names_in_label_order.tsv


These files contain the corresponding fixed-length representations, masks, and TF ordering information for the transcription factors held out from training.

The unseen-TF representations are used exclusively for zero-shot evaluation.

TF Protein Processing Workflow

The TF protein data follow the general processing workflow:



Amino-acid sequences
        ↓
     ProstT5
        ↓
sequence-based representations

Protein structures
        ↓
     Foldseek
        ↓
3Di structural sequences
        ↓
structure-aware representations

Sequence + structural representations
        ↓
fixed-length processing
        ↓
200-token TF representations
        ↓
seen TF / unseen TF sets


Seen and unseen TFs are processed together during the initial protein preprocessing stages. They are separated only at the final fixed-length representation stage used by the model.

Cached DNA–TF Pair Indices (cached_pairs/)

To facilitate reproducible training and evaluation and reduce repeated sampling during data loading, this release includes pre-generated DNA–TF pair indices under cached_pairs/.

Cached pairs are provided for five random seeds:



seed42

seed86

seed123

seed666

seed2026


Each seed directory contains separate cached pairs for the seen- and unseen-TF evaluation settings:



cached_pairs/
├── seed42/
│   ├── seentf/
│   │   ├── train_pairs.npy
│   │   ├── val_pairs.npy
│   │   └── test_pairs.npy
│   └── unseentf/
│       └── test_pairs.npy
├── seed86/
├── seed123/
├── seed666/
└── seed2026/


For the seen-TF setting, cached DNA–TF pair indices are provided for the training, validation, and test datasets. All positive DNA–TF pairs are retained, while negative pairs are sampled using predefined sampling fractions. The training, validation, and test cached pairs use negative sampling fractions of 0.003, 0.5, and 1.0, respectively.

For the unseen-TF setting, only test_pairs.npy is provided because the eight held-out TFs are excluded from training and validation and are used exclusively for zero-shot evaluation. The unseen-TF test set uses all available DNA–TF pairs, corresponding to a negative sampling fraction of 1.0.

Each *_pairs.npy file stores pre-generated DNA–TF index pairs identifying the DNA sequence and TF/task combinations used in the corresponding experiment.

Pair sampling is independently generated for each of the five specified random seeds. The cached pair files allow the same sampled DNA–TF combinations to be reused across runs, improving reproducibility and avoiding the need to regenerate sampling indices each time the dataset is loaded.

Intended Use

This dataset is intended for:



Training and evaluating TF–DNA binding prediction models

Reproducing the experiments reported in the revised TFBindFormer study

Evaluating zero-shot generalization to unseen transcription factors

Studying protein-conditioned DNA-binding specificity

Investigating sequence- and structure-aware TF representations

Developing multimodal models integrating genomic DNA sequence, TF protein information, and cell-type context

Reproducing multi-seed experiments using pre-generated DNA–TF sampling indices


The dataset is provided for research and academic use and is intended to support reproducible model training and evaluation within the TFBindFormer framework.

seen_tf_metadata.tsv – metadata for TF–cell-type tasks associated with transcription factors represented during model training.

unseen_tf_metadata.tsv – metadata for TF–cell-type tasks associated with transcription factors excluded from training and reserved for zero-shot evaluation.

seen_cell_type_ids.npy – encoded cell-type identifiers corresponding to the seen-TF tasks.

unseen_cell_type_ids.npy – encoded cell-type identifiers corresponding to the unseen-TF tasks.


The metadata files provide mappings among transcription factors, cell types or experimental conditions, and their corresponding prediction tasks.

The revised TFBindFormer dataset contains:



100 seen TFs, corresponding to 422 TF–cell-type tasks

8 unseen TFs, corresponding to 35 TF–cell-type tasks


The unseen TFs are completely excluded from model training and are used exclusively to evaluate zero-shot generalization to previously unseen transcription factors.

Transcription Factor Data (tf_data/)

The tf_data directory contains TF protein sequence, structural, and processed representation data used by the TFBindFormer protein encoder.

Amino-Acid Sequences (aa_sequences/)

The aa_sequences directory contains amino-acid FASTA sequences for all seen and unseen TFs included in the dataset.

These protein sequences provide the sequence information used to generate pretrained TF representations.

Protein Structures (pdb_structures/)

The pdb_structures directory contains protein structure files in PDB format for all seen and unseen TFs.

These structures are used to derive Foldseek 3Di structural representations.

Foldseek 3Di Structural Sequences (foldseek_3Di_ss.fasta)

foldseek_3Di_ss.fasta contains precomputed Foldseek 3Di structural token sequences derived from the TF protein structures.

The 3Di representation converts local three-dimensional protein environments into discrete structural tokens, providing structure-aware information that complements amino-acid sequence information.

ProstT5 Embeddings (prostt5_embeddings/)

The prostt5_embeddings directory contains precomputed TF protein embeddings for the seen and unseen TFs generated using ProstT5-based sequence and structural representations.

These embeddings are stored before conversion to the fixed-length protein representations used directly by TFBindFormer.

Fixed-Length TF Representations (fixed_length_200/)

TF proteins vary in sequence length. Before being provided to the TFBindFormer model, their protein representations are standardized to a fixed length of 200 tokens.

The fixed_length_200 directory contains the final model-ready TF representations and is divided into seen- and unseen-TF sets.

Seen TFs (fixed_length_200/seen_tf/)



fixed_tf_embs.pt

fixed_tf_masks.pt

tf_names_in_label_order.tsv


fixed_tf_embs.pt contains the fixed-length protein embeddings for TFs represented during model training.

fixed_tf_masks.pt contains the corresponding masks used to distinguish valid protein-token positions from padded positions.

tf_names_in_label_order.tsv records the TF ordering corresponding to the protein tensors and TF-binding label ordering. This file ensures that each protein representation is correctly matched to its corresponding prediction task.

Unseen TFs (fixed_length_200/unseen_tf/)



fixed_tf_embs.pt

fixed_tf_masks.pt

tf_names_in_label_order.tsv


These files contain the corresponding fixed-length representations, masks, and TF ordering information for the transcription factors held out from training.

The unseen-TF representations are used exclusively for zero-shot evaluation.

TF Protein Processing Workflow

The TF protein data follow the general processing workflow:



Amino-acid sequences
        ↓
     ProstT5
        ↓
sequence-based representations

Protein structures
        ↓
     Foldseek
        ↓
3Di structural sequences
        ↓
structure-aware representations

Sequence + structural representations
        ↓
fixed-length processing
        ↓
200-token TF representations
        ↓
seen TF / unseen TF sets


Seen and unseen TFs are processed together during the initial protein preprocessing stages. They are separated only at the final fixed-length representation stage used by the model.

Cached DNA–TF Pair Indices (cached_pairs/)

To facilitate reproducible training and evaluation and reduce repeated sampling during data loading, this release includes pre-generated DNA–TF pair indices under cached_pairs/.

Cached pairs are provided for five random seeds:



seed42

seed86

seed123

seed666

seed2026


Each seed directory contains separate cached pairs for the seen- and unseen-TF evaluation settings:



cached_pairs/
├── seed42/
│   ├── seentf/
│   │   ├── train_pairs.npy
│   │   ├── val_pairs.npy
│   │   └── test_pairs.npy
│   └── unseentf/
│       └── test_pairs.npy
├── seed86/
├── seed123/
├── seed666/
└── seed2026/


For the seen-TF setting, cached DNA–TF pair indices are provided for the training, validation, and test datasets. All positive DNA–TF pairs are retained, while negative pairs are sampled using predefined sampling fractions. The training, validation, and test cached pairs use negative sampling fractions of 0.003, 0.5, and 1.0, respectively.

For the unseen-TF setting, only test_pairs.npy is provided because the eight held-out TFs are excluded from training and validation and are used exclusively for zero-shot evaluation. The unseen-TF test set uses all available DNA–TF pairs, corresponding to a negative sampling fraction of 1.0.

Each *_pairs.npy file stores pre-generated DNA–TF index pairs identifying the DNA sequence and TF/task combinations used in the corresponding experiment.

Pair sampling is independently generated for each of the five specified random seeds. The cached pair files allow the same sampled DNA–TF combinations to be reused across runs, improving reproducibility and avoiding the need to regenerate sampling indices each time the dataset is loaded.

Intended Use

This dataset is intended for:



Training and evaluating TF–DNA binding prediction models

Reproducing the experiments reported in the revised TFBindFormer study

Evaluating zero-shot generalization to unseen transcription factors

Studying protein-conditioned DNA-binding specificity

Investigating sequence- and structure-aware TF representations

Developing multimodal models integrating genomic DNA sequence, TF protein information, and cell-type context

Reproducing multi-seed experiments using pre-generated DNA–TF sampling indices


The dataset is provided for research and academic use and is intended to support reproducible model training and evaluation within the TFBindFormer framework.

titles.title: Alignment depth and the structure prediction of partner proteins of phage reverse transcriptases: data for checking the reported results

descriptions.description:
Data accompanying the manuscript "Low confidence is not absence: what alignment depth lets structure prediction say about partner proteins of phage reverse transcriptases" (Pyo, AI3 Discovery).
The deposit is deliberately minimal: it contains what is needed to check and re-derive the results reported in the manuscript. Contents: README.md (layout and verification); manuscript_en.pdf and manuscript_ko.pdf (English and Korean versions of the manuscript); core.tar.gz (figures, the number files NUMBERS.json and NUMBERS_D13.json, the sequences of all analysed proteins, per-stage result tables, and integrity records: the SHA-256 of every file, the verifier verify_release.py, hash commitments for the pre-registration documents and for the withheld files); one <stage>.tar.gz with its <stage>.members.sha256 for each analysis stage (predicted structures in PDB format from AlphaFold2-multimer v3 and Boltz-2, the multiple sequence alignments given to the predictors, confidence outputs, Foldseek hit tables, per-window score tables); CHECKSUMS_TOPLEVEL.sha256.
Analysis and scoring code, calibrated threshold files and the texts of the pre-registration documents are not deposited; their SHA-256 hashes and git commit identifiers are included so that they can be checked if they are disclosed later. All structures are predictions; no claim about enzymatic activity is made. The git history behind the commitments is a local record without an external timestamp; the date of this deposit is the first external timestamp.
To verify: download all files into one folder, run tar xzf core.tar.gz, then python3 integrity/verify_release.py . (standard library only). Public inputs used and not redistributed: ColabFold server alignments, Logan protein clusters (s3://logan-pub), PDB entries, Pfam-A 38.2. Third-party tools and data keep their own licenses.

titles.title: Data for: Three correctable biases inflate estimates of structural novelty from predicted-structure databases

descriptions.description:
Derived data supporting the manuscript Three correctable biases inflate estimates of structural novelty from predicted-structure databases.

Contents: per-protein structural-novelty calls for 135,523 proteins across 15 eukaryotic proteomes, with best Foldseek target, TM-score, mean pLDDT and novelty verdict; PDB100 re-verification of all 8,011 confidently novel hypothetical proteins in the panel, with per-protein reassignments and own-genus flags; US-align re-scoring of the 137 Plasmodium falciparum candidates; self-match counts for the five-organism comparison; and the AlphaFold Database dark-cluster re-analysis for releases v3 and v6.

Proteome accessions and taxon identifiers were verified against the UniProt REST API on 22 September 2026 and are pinned rather than resolved at runtime. Foldseek 8.ef4e960 was used for forward searches against AlphaFold/Swiss-Prot and 10.941cd33 for PDB100 (release 2025-01-01).

The raw Foldseek alignment output (20.9 million rows, ~1.6 GB) is not deposited; it regenerates from the analysis code and the pinned panel, and is available from the author on request.

Analysis code: https://github.com/ktosmanprotein/structural-novelty-bias (MIT). The AlphaFold Database cluster data re-analysed here were published by Barrio-Hernandez et al., Nature 2023, under CC-BY 4.0.

titles.title: Data from: Fragment morphometry analysis and same-color-channel separation enable objective quantification across BBB models

descriptions.description:
Quantifying blood-brain barrier (BBB) integrity from fluorescence
 microscopy remains limited by subjective scoring and categorical
 classification methods that lack reproducibility. For objective and
 consistent BBB phenotyping, we present two semi-automated image-analysis
 pipelines that replace manual scoring with quantitative,
 continuous-variable measurements. Our in vitro pipeline, implemented in
 Python, quantifies the connectivity of tight junction structures by
 measuring discrete ZO-1 fragment objects within manually traced junction
 regions. It outputs continuous metrics including average fragment area,
 total junctional area, and a junctional fragmentation ratio that captures
 the degree of ZO‑1 continuity versus discontinuity. In human brain
 microvascular endothelial cells subjected to glycocalyx component
 knockdown, the pipeline detected significantly reduced fragment area (37%
 decrease for both CD44 and syndecan-1 (SDC1) knockdown, p = 0.0148 and
 0.0084) and junctional fragmentation ratio (p = 0.0061 and 0.0137). Our in
 vivo pipeline integrates ilastik-based pixel classification with FIJI
 macro automation to quantify vascular marker colocalization and to
 separate vessel signal from microglial contamination within a single
 fluorescence channel, eliminating the need for dedicated counterstains.
 Applied across four mouse cohorts [young, aged, Alzheimer's,
 traumatic brain injury (TBI)] and three brain regions [prefrontal cortex
 (PFC), hippocampus, midbrain], the pipeline revealed concurrent ZO-1 loss
 and ICAM-1 elevation in the PFC and hippocampus of aged and
 Alzheimer's mice, with Alzheimer's-specific doubling of eNOS
 occurring in the PFC (p = 0.0013). TBI mice showed persistent ZO-1 loss
 with transient ICAM-1 and eNOS changes. Both deterministic pipelines are
 available on GitHub and designed for adoption beyond the specific markers
 and systems analyzed here.

# Data from: Fragment morphometry analysis and same-color-channel
 separation enable reproducible, continuous-variable quantification across
 BBB models Benjamin D. Peck, Nicholas R. O'Hare, Craig F. Ferris,
 Rebecca L. Pinals, Eno E. Ebong Correspondence and for any queries
 regarding the dataset, please reach out to the corresponding author at:
 Eno E. Ebong, [e.ebong@northeastern.edu](mailto:e.ebong@northeastern.edu)
 Dataset
 DOI: [https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.s7h44j1qd](https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.s7h44j1qd) ## Description of the data and file structure This dataset contains the per-image quantitative outputs underlying two fluorescence microscopy analyses of blood-brain barrier integrity. One analysis is in vitro, measuring ZO-1 tight junction fragmentation in cultured endothelial cells under glycocalyx knockdown. The other is in vivo, measuring three vascular markers within tomato-lectin-defined brain vessels across mouse cohorts. The data are provided as a single Excel workbook with four sheets. Each row in every sheet is one image, and all values are raw pipeline outputs rather than aggregated statistics. The grouped per-replicate and per-cohort tables used for statistical testing were derived from these sheets by averaging within groups and were therefore not included. There are no missing or empty cells in any sheet. The source images are multi-channel confocal Z-stacks in Zeiss CZI format and are not included. The analyses described in the manuscript can be reproduced from the workbook alone. ### Files and variables #### File: Peck_OHare_Ebong_2026_BBB_quantification.xlsx | Sheet name | Description | Rows | | :------------- | :----------------------------------------------------------------------- | :--- | | ZO-1 in vitro | Image-level quantification of in vitro ZO-1 tight junction fragmentation | 42 | | ZO-1 in vivo | Image-level quantification of in vivo ZO-1 coverage on vessels | 42 | | ICAM-1 in vivo | Image-level quantification of in vivo ICAM-1 coverage on vessels | 42 | | eNOS in vivo | Image-level quantification of in vivo eNOS coverage on vessels | 42 | The workbook has four sheets. The in vitro sheet has its own column structure, and the three in vivo sheets share an identical 29-column structure. All values are raw, image-level pipeline outputs rather than aggregated statistics. There are no missing or empty cells in any sheet. ##### Sheet: ZO-1 in vitro **Description:** This file contains per-image quantification of ZO-1 tight junction morphology in human brain microvascular endothelial cells (HBMECs). Three conditions were compared: a GFP control and two glycocalyx knockdowns targeting CD44 and syndecan-1. Each condition has biological replicates with three images each. In the filename, Z and V denote the ZO-1 and VE-cadherin channels, and the condition uses the codes below. CD44 knockdown replicate 3 was excluded before analysis because of insufficient ZO-1 and VE-cadherin signal. There are no blank cells in this sheet. | Condition | Code in filename | Replicates | Images | | :------------------- | :--------------- | :--------- | :----- | | GFP control | GFP | 1 to 5 | 15 | | CD44 knockdown | CD44KD | 1, 2, 4, 5 | 12 | | Syndecan-1 knockdown | SDCKD | 1 to 5 | 15 | Column definitions: | Column | Description | Units | | :------------------------ | :---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | :----------------- | | filename | image identifier, HBMEC\_\[condition]\_Z\_V\_\[replicate]\_\[image] | text | | filtered\_fragments | number of ZO-1 junction fragments retained after size filtering | count | | avg\_fragment\_area\_um | mean area of retained fragments | square micrometers | | total\_junction\_area\_um | total junctional area in the image | square micrometers | | final\_pixels | junction-positive pixel count after filtering | pixels | | original\_pixels | junction-positive pixel count before filtering | pixels | | junctional\_ratio | junctional ratio, fraction of junction-positive pixels retained after filtering, equal to final\_pixels divided by original\_pixels | fraction, 0 to 1 | | adaptive\_threshold | intensity threshold applied to the junction channel | 16-bit grey value | | background\_mean | mean background intensity of the junction channel | 16-bit grey value | ##### Sheets: ZO-1 in vivo, ICAM-1 in vivo, eNOS in vivo **Description:** These three sheets contain per-image quantification of three vascular markers in female mouse brain tissue, measured within tomato-lectin-defined vessels. They share an identical 29-column structure, one sheet per marker. Four cohorts were sampled across three brain regions, with four animals per cohort and region except the TBI control, which has two. TBI was a descriptive positive control and was not included in the statistical comparisons. The primary measured variable is *percent_coverage_on_vessels*. The dextran columns were retained for structural consistency but are zero throughout, as dextran was not part of this analysis. The filename tokens use the same codes as the protein, mouse_type, brain_region, and sample_number columns. There are no blank cells in these sheets. | Cohort code | Meaning | | :---------- | :---------------------------------------------------------- | | YOUNG | young, 3 months, C57BL/6 | | OLD | aged, 18 months, C57BL/6 | | AD | Alzheimer's disease, 18 months, APPswe/PSEN1dE9 on C57BL/6 | | TBI | traumatic brain injury, positive control, 3 months, C57BL/6 | | Region code | Meaning | | :---------- | :---------------- | | PFC | prefrontal cortex | | HIPP | hippocampus | | MID | midbrain | Column definitions: | Column | Description | Units | | :----------------------------- | :---------------------------------------------------------------- | :-------------------- | | filename | image identifier, \[marker]\_\[cohort]\_\[region]\_\[sample] | text | | protein | marker imaged (eNOS, ZO-1, ICAM) | text | | magnification | objective magnification | text | | mouse\_type | cohort, see cohort codes above | text | | brain\_region | region, see region codes above | text | | sample\_number | replicate index within cohort and region | integer | | mouse\_id | cohort and replicate identifier | text | | vessel\_area\_percent | image area classified as vessel from the lectin mask | percent | | mean\_intensity | mean marker-channel intensity within the analyzed region | 16-bit grey value | | protein\_coverage\_percent | image area positive for the marker | percent | | percent\_coverage\_on\_vessels | vessel area positive for the marker, primary analysis variable | percent | | dextran\_coverage\_percent | dextran channel coverage, not used in this analysis, all values 0 | percent | | dextran\_total\_percent | dextran total coverage, not used in this analysis, all values 0 | percent | | bg\_mean | mean background intensity of the marker channel | 16-bit grey value | | bg\_median | median background intensity of the marker channel | 16-bit grey value | | bg\_std | standard deviation of background intensity | 16-bit grey value | | bg\_threshold | intensity threshold applied to the marker channel | 16-bit grey value | | roi\_x | analysis region origin, x | pixels | | roi\_y | analysis region origin, y | pixels | | roi\_width | analysis region width | pixels | | roi\_height | analysis region height | pixels | | roi\_area | analysis region area | square micrometers | | original\_width | source image width | pixels | | original\_height | source image height | pixels | | meta\_magnification | objective magnification from image metadata | text | | meta\_pixel\_size\_um | pixel size from image metadata | micrometers per pixel | | meta\_objective | objective from image metadata | text | | meta\_tile\_scan | whether the image is a tile scan | Yes or No | | meta\_bit\_depth | image bit depth | bits | ZO-1 images were acquired at 40x and ICAM-1 at 20x. eNOS images were acquired at 20x or 40x depending on cohort and animal, with the per-image value recorded in the magnification and meta_magnification columns. Pixel size also varies by acquisition and is recorded per image in *meta_pixel_size_um*. ##### Abbreviations * HBMEC: human brain microvascular endothelial cell * ZO-1: zonula occludens-1, tight junction protein * ICAM-1: intercellular adhesion molecule 1 * eNOS: endothelial nitric oxide synthase * CD44: cluster of differentiation 44, a glycocalyx core protein * SDC1: syndecan-1, a glycocalyx core protein * GFP: green fluorescent protein, control condition * AD: Alzheimer's disease * TBI: traumatic brain injury * ROI: region of interest ## Code/software All data files can be viewed or reanalyzed using freely available, open-source,e or commonly accessible software. No proprietary programs are required to read the data. ### General viewing The workbook can be opened in Microsoft Excel or Google Sheets, and the sheets can be read directly in R or Python. No specialized software is required to view or interpret the numeric data. ### Data analysis and quantification workflow #### In vitro ZO-1 fragmentation Source code, version 1.0: [https://github.com/peckbe/junction-fragmentation-analysis](https://github.com/peckbe/junction-fragmentation-analysis) Software: Python 3.12.3, with bioio 3.2.0, numpy 2.4.2, scipy 1.17.1, scikit-image 0.26.0, opencv-python 4.13.0, Pillow 12.1.1, pandas 3.0.0, and matplotlib 3.10.8. Workflow: 1. Acquire ZO-1 and VE-cadherin confocal images on a Zeiss LSM 800 with a 63x/1.4 NA oil objective. 2. In the 01_export_projections notebook, project each CZI by maximum intensity and export a ZO-1 and VE-cadherin composite. 3. Trace junction regions manually on the composite, using VE-cadherin as reference. 4. In the 02_import_tracings notebook, split the traced outlines into per-image files. 5. The 03_fragment_analysis notebook builds a binary mask from each tracing, applies adaptive background correction, filters and labels fragments, measures fragment area, total junctional area, and junctional ratio, then exports the results to CSV. #### In vivo vessel colocalization Source code, version 1.0: [https://github.com/peckbe/ilastik-fiji-colocalization](https://github.com/peckbe/ilastik-fiji-colocalization) Software: ilastik 1.4.1.post1-gpu for pixel classification, FIJI/ImageJ 1.54p run through a macro built into the notebook, and Python 3.12.3, with bioio 3.2.0, numpy 2.4.2, pandas 3.0.0, tifffile 2026.1.28, h5py 3.15.1, and matplotlib 3.10.8. Workflow: 1. Acquire confocal images of each marker with tomato lectin co-stain using 40x/1.4 NA oil or 20x/0.8 NA air. 2. Train a three-class ilastik pixel classifier (vessel, microglia, background) on the tomato lectin co-stain channel to separate vessel from microglial signal. 3. In the ilastik_fiji_colocalization notebook, export the tomato lectin Z-stacks, run headless ilastik prediction with the trained classifier, and generate three cleaned vessel variants (binary, probability-weighted, dominant-class). 4. A built-in FIJI macro applies rolling-ball background subtraction, a maximum intensity projection, vessel masking from the tomato lectin channel, and Otsu thresholding to set marker coverage, then exports the results to CSV. ### Statistical analysis GraphPad Prism 11.0.2, or open-source equivalents such as R or JASP, can reproduce the analyses from the per-image values. The in vitro data were compared by one-way ANOVA with Tukey post-hoc after averaging per flow experiment. For the in vivo data, each marker was analyzed by two-way ANOVA, cohort by brain region, with Tukey post-hoc on the regional measurements, and by one-way ANOVA on the global averages. The TBI cohort was excluded from the statistical model and shown descriptively. ## Access information Source Images: * Because of their size, the source images are not easily publicized and are not available in this or any other repository. They are able to be replicated based on information shared in the manuscript article, which describes the staining, acquisition, and processing parameters, and in the pipeline repositories listed above. Other publicly accessible locations of the data: * None Data were derived from the following sources: * None ### Data integrity and reuse All numeric values are provided within an Excel (.xlsx) workbook. No macros, merged cells, or embedded figures are included. Each sheet is a single flat table suitable for reanalysis in R, Python, or spreadsheet environments. Users may reuse these data for meta-analyses, benchmarking of endothelial and cerebrovascular marker quantification, or integration with other vascular datasets.

titles.title: Co-folding confidence scores do not order the substrates of threonyl-tRNA synthetase, and a trained affinity head only partly does: data, code and manuscript

affiliation: Department of Chemistry and Physics, McNeese State University, Lake Charles, LA, USA
creators.name: Boggavarapu, Kiran

descriptions.description:
Complete data, code and manuscript for the preprint of the same title. Three co-folding models (AlphaFold3, Protenix, Boltz-2) on two orthologous constructs (Escherichia coli and Saccharomyces cerevisiae threonyl-tRNA synthetase), tested against published discrimination factors for 19 of the 20 amino acids. Includes all predictions, derived per-substrate and per-seed tables, measured kinetics, analysis code, and a self-checking verify_all.py that re-derives 173 reported values from the deposited tables using the Python standard library alone and exits non-zero on any disagreement.
What it shows. (1) No confidence readout orders the 18 non-cognate substrates. Rank correlations against the binding-step discrimination factor I' run from -0.143 to +0.133, and pairwise ordering is correct for 45 to 54 per cent of untied substrate pairs. (2) All nine confidence readouts instead place serine in the bottom three of 18 by predicted rejection, six of them last, and serine is the non-cognate this enzyme rejects best at the binding step. (3) The top-ranked predicted structures give a measured account of that case: serine's hydroxyl oxygen sits 2.138 A from the catalytic zinc and threonine's sits 2.167 A, and after superposition the two oxygens lie 0.202 A apart, so the models place the discriminating atom correctly and then score the complex as though placing it were the whole problem. (4) Boltz-2's trained affinity head carries the correct sign in both species (rho = +0.470 and +0.358 against I') with no steric confound (partial rho given volume +0.458 and +0.361), and still places serine eighth and fifteenth. (5) Each model reproduces its own substrate ordering across the two orthologues far better than it matches the enzyme (rho = +0.73 to +0.86, against rho near zero agreement with measured discrimination). (6) An AlphaFold3 zinc-ligand knock-out collapses the threonine-over-valine preference by 0.112 (95% CI 0.106-0.117) and inverts it, with no change in predicted fold, so the readouts are not blind to catalysis.
Changes from the previous version. Adds the Protenix arm, the species-matched yeast arm for both AlphaFold3 and Boltz-2, a structural figure measured from the top-ranked models, and the cross-orthologue reproducibility analysis. Withdraws the mechanistic reading of the two-head difference within Boltz-2: tested with Williams' test for dependent correlations sharing a criterion it gives p = 0.191, and the species-matched replicate does not reproduce the gap. Corrects every confidence interval, which had used the Pearson standard error 1/sqrt(n-3) rather than the 1.06/sqrt(n-3) appropriate to a Spearman rho, making each about 6 per cent too narrow.
Measured discrimination factors are transcribed with attribution from Freist, Sternbach & Cramer (1994) Eur J Biochem 220:745-752, doi:10.1111/j.1432-1033.1994.tb18675.x. Residue volumes from Zamyatnin (1972) Prog Biophys Mol Biol 24:107-123. Boltz-2 from Passaro et al. (2025), doi:10.1101/2025.06.14.659707.

verify_all.py runs on the Python standard library alone, re-derives 173 reported values from the deposited tables and exits non-zero on any disagreement. mutation_test.py corrupts one deposited cell at a time and confirms the verifier catches each one.

(2) All nine confidence readouts instead place serine in the bottom three of 18 by predicted rejection, six of them last, and serine is the non-cognate this enzyme rejects best at the binding step. (3) The top-ranked predicted structures give a measured account of that case: serine's hydroxyl oxygen sits 2.138 A from the catalytic zinc and threonine's sits 2.167 A, and after superposition the two oxygens lie 0.202 A apart, so the models place the discriminating atom correctly and then score the complex as though placing it were the whole problem. (4) Boltz-2's trained affinity head carries the correct sign in both species (rho = +0.470 and +0.358 against I') with no steric confound (partial rho given volume +0.458 and +0.361), and still places serine eighth and fifteenth. (5) Each model reproduces its own substrate ordering across the two orthologues far better than it matches the enzyme (rho = +0.73 to +0.86, against rho near zero agreement with measured discrimination). (6) An AlphaFold3 zinc-ligand knock-out collapses the threonine-over-valine preference by 0.112 (95% CI 0.106-0.117) and inverts it, with no change in predicted fold, so the readouts are not blind to catalysis.
Changes from the previous version. Adds the Protenix arm, the species-matched yeast arm for both AlphaFold3 and Boltz-2, a structural figure measured from the top-ranked models, and the cross-orthologue reproducibility analysis. Withdraws the mechanistic reading of the two-head difference within Boltz-2: tested with Williams' test for dependent correlations sharing a criterion it gives p = 0.191, and the species-matched replicate does not reproduce the gap. Corrects every confidence interval, which had used the Pearson standard error 1/sqrt(n-3) rather than the 1.06/sqrt(n-3) appropriate to a Spearman rho, making each about 6 per cent too narrow.
Measured discrimination factors are transcribed with attribution from Freist, Sternbach & Cramer (1994) Eur J Biochem 220:745-752, doi:10.1111/j.1432-1033.1994.tb18675.x. Residue volumes from Zamyatnin (1972) Prog Biophys Mol Biol 24:107-123. Boltz-2 from Passaro et al. (2025), doi:10.1101/2025.06.14.659707.

titles.title: Hi-PPI: Highly accurate prediction of stable protein–protein interactions via integrating sequence semantics and structure-aware representations

descriptions.description:
Production model checkpoints and template resources used by the template-assisted Hi-PPI protein–protein interaction distance/contact prediction workflow.
This snapshot contains 34,231 template PDB structures, the corresponding Foldseek database and index files, and the original deposition-date JSON. The archive contains 34,246 files, totaling 1,621,308,576 bytes before compression. All Foldseek lookup template IDs have matching PDB files. Seventeen template IDs lack dates in the supplied mapping and are skipped by the existing Hi-PPI search code. The original data are preserved; a date cutoff is applied at search time rather than to this archive.
Files include the compressed database, SHA256SUMS for integrity verification, and a README with extraction and Hi-PPI usage instructions. This version adds the production checkpoints hi_ppi_no_template.pkl and hi_ppi_template.pkl, with SHA-256 checksums in WEIGHTS_SHA256SUMS. Foldseek and US-align executables and sequence/AlphaFold databases are not included.
Associated software: Hi-PPI.

titles.title: Data from: Integrative discovery and functional dependency mapping uncover essential chimeric RNAs in the active transcriptome

descriptions.description:
Chimeric RNAs are a diverse class of molecules defined as RNA transcripts
 containing genetic information for multiple genes that arise from both
 DNA-level and RNA-level fusion events. While their expression patterns
 across various tissue types and disease states have been well-documented,
 the biological function of these transcripts remains poorly understood. In
 this study, we developed an integrative prediction
 pipeline to establish a comprehensive atlas of 569,640 chimeric
 RNAs across 1,019 cancer cell lines, providing the high-resolution
 landscape required for functional interrogation. Leveraging this resource,
 we performed a systematic functional dependency
 screen by integrating our predictions with large-scale RNAi
 datasets from The Cancer Dependency Map (DepMap) project. This
 approach moves beyond simple chimeric RNA prediction to identify
 high-confidence chimeric RNAs essential for cell viability, including a
 previously uncharacterized class of recurrent chimeric transcripts likely
 generated by cis-splicing of adjacent genes (cis-SAGe) found across wide
 varieties of tissue types and disease states. We demonstrate that
 depletion of selected candidate chimeras disrupts cell cycle progression
 and cellular fitness and that these transcripts are frequently
 dysregulated in primary breast tumors, highlighting their potential
 biological relevance and clinical significance. Together, these results
 demonstrate that chimeric RNAs constitute a previously underappreciated
 layer of gene expression, effectively expanding the repertoire of the
 functional genome beyond conventional genetics. By prioritizing function,
 this study establishes a framework for investigating biologically relevant
 chimeric transcripts and highlights their potential as therapeutic targets
 and biomarkers in cancer.

# Data from: Integrative discovery and functional dependency mapping
 uncover essential chimeric RNAs in the active transcriptome Dataset DOI:
 [10.5061/dryad.fxpnvx18g](https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.fxpnvx18g) ##
 Description of the data and file structure Dataset Overview This dataset
 accompanies the manuscript: "Integrative Discovery and Functional
 Dependency Mapping Uncover Essential Chimeric RNAs in the Active
 Transcriptome." The repository contains datasets, source data, raw
 experimental data, and analysis scripts used to identify, characterize,
 and evaluate the functional significance of chimeric RNAs across cancer
 cell lines and breast cancer patient cohorts. The deposited materials
 include: \- Chimeric RNA predictions across Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia
 (CCLE) cell lines. \- Functional genomic screening data integrated from
 the Cancer Dependency Map (DepMap). \- Identification of essential and
 non-essential cis-splicing of adjacent gene (cis-SAGe) chimeric RNAs. \-
 Gene set enrichment analyses (GSEA). \- Long-read sequencing analyses. \-
 Mass spectrometry analyses. \- Nonsense-mediated decay (NMD) predictions.
 \- Subcellular localization analyses. \- Breast cancer (TCGA-BRCA)
 chimeric RNA predictions and associated clinical analyses. \- Survival and
 subtype-specific investigations. \- Source data underlying manuscript
 figures. \- Raw western blot data. \- Analysis scripts used to generate

titles.title: Dual role of CsrA in regulating the hemolytic activity of Escherichia coli O157:H7

descriptions.description: Post-transcriptional global carbon storage regulator A (CsrA) is a sequence-specific RNA-binding protein involved in the regulation of multiple bacterial processes. Hemolysin is an important virulence factor in the enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli O157:H7 (EHEC). Here, we show that CsrA plays a dual role in the regulation of hemolysis in EHEC. CsrA significantly represses plasmid-borne enterohemolysin (EhxA)-mediated hemolysis and activates chromosome-borne hemolysin E (HlyE)-mediated hemolysis through different mechanisms. RNA structure prediction revealed a well-matched stem-loop structure with two potential CsrA binding sites located on the 5' untranslated region (UTR) of ehxB, which encodes a translocator required for EhxA secretion. CsrA inhibits EhxA secretion by directly binding to the RNA leader sequence of ehxB to repress its expression in two different ways: CsrA either binds to the Shine–Dalgarno sequence of ehxB to block ribosome access or to ehxB transcript to promote its mRNA decay. The predicted CsrA-binding site 1 of ehxB is essential for its regulation. There is a single potential CsrA-binding site at the 5'-end of the hlyE transcript, and its mutation completely abolishes CsrA-dependent activation. CsrA can also stabilize hlyE mRNA by directly binding to its 5' UTR. Overall, our results indicate that CsrA acts as a hemolysis modulator to regulate pathogenicity under certain conditions.

titles.title: Dual role of CsrA in regulating the hemolytic activity of Escherichia coli O157:H7

descriptions.description: Post-transcriptional global carbon storage regulator A (CsrA) is a sequence-specific RNA-binding protein involved in the regulation of multiple bacterial processes. Hemolysin is an important virulence factor in the enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli O157:H7 (EHEC). Here, we show that CsrA plays a dual role in the regulation of hemolysis in EHEC. CsrA significantly represses plasmid-borne enterohemolysin (EhxA)-mediated hemolysis and activates chromosome-borne hemolysin E (HlyE)-mediated hemolysis through different mechanisms. RNA structure prediction revealed a well-matched stem-loop structure with two potential CsrA binding sites located on the 5' untranslated region (UTR) of ehxB, which encodes a translocator required for EhxA secretion. CsrA inhibits EhxA secretion by directly binding to the RNA leader sequence of ehxB to repress its expression in two different ways: CsrA either binds to the Shine–Dalgarno sequence of ehxB to block ribosome access or to ehxB transcript to promote its mRNA decay. The predicted CsrA-binding site 1 of ehxB is essential for its regulation. There is a single potential CsrA-binding site at the 5'-end of the hlyE transcript, and its mutation completely abolishes CsrA-dependent activation. CsrA can also stabilize hlyE mRNA by directly binding to its 5' UTR. Overall, our results indicate that CsrA acts as a hemolysis modulator to regulate pathogenicity under certain conditions.

titles.title: Large-scale analysis of AlphaFold structures reveals organism-specific physicochemical signatures

descriptions.description:
Data for: Large-scale analysis of AlphaFold structures reveals organism-specific physicochemical signatures

This record contains the input data needed to reproduce the analysis in the paper above. The analysis code is at https://github.com/wells-wood-research/proteinPropertiesReconstructTreeOfLife, and the repository README explains how to use these files. To set up the data, run `bash scripts/setup_data.sh RECORD_ID` from the repository root. It downloads these files and places each one where the scripts expect it.

Files

Tree of Life analysis 

destress_data.zip - DE-STRESS metrics [1] (about 70 structural features per model) for 564,446 AlphaFold2 [2] models of the proteomes of 48 organisms (AlphaFold DB v4) [3] and for 216,681 experimentally determined PDB structures [4] (downloaded June 2024). Contains `destress_data_af2.csv` and `destress_data_pdb_082024.csv`.af2_plddt_scores.csv - Mean pLDDT for each AlphaFold2 model, calculated from the C-alpha atom B-factor values in the AlphaFold DB PDB files. Models with mean pLDDT < 70 are removed in the analysis.filtered_af2db_clusters_data.csv - AlphaFold DB FoldSeek cluster assignments (cluster representative, UniProt ID, cluster flag, taxon ID) for the proteins in the data set. Filtered from the AFDB cluster membership table [5].uniprot_results_org_subcellloc_uniprotkb.csv - Organism, subcellular location, GO terms and gene encoding type for each protein, from the UniProt REST API (snapshot downloaded November 2024) [6].af2db_org_uniprot_desc_results.csv - Organism name and UniProt description for each protein, from the AlphaFold DB REST API (snapshot downloaded October 2024) [3].af2_structures_non_redundant.csv - The non-redundant list of 251,376 structures (one randomly selected structure per organism and FoldSeek cluster representative, random seed 42) [5].ncbi_phylo_tree.phy and ncbi_phylo_tree_euk.phy - Reference phylogenies in Newick format for all 48 organisms and for the 31 eukaryotes, created with the Common Tree tool of the NCBI Taxonomy Browser [7].randomTreeDistances.rda - Pre-computed distances between random pairs of bifurcating trees, used as the null model for the Clustering Information Distance (CID). This is the `randomTreeDistances` object from the R data package TreeDistData (Smith, https://github.com/ms609/TreeDistData). It is an array of 24 tree-distance methods x 13 summary statistics (min, percentiles, max, mean, sd) x 197 leaf counts (4 to 200); the analysis uses the "cid" entries. It is used with the R package TreeDist (10.32614/CRAN.package.TreeDist) [8], which was also used to calculate the CID between the DE-STRESS trees and the NCBI trees. The file is included for convenience and is not our work; please cite TreeDist/TreeDistData if you use it.

scFv antibody analysis

fleishman_antibody_expression_data.csv - Yeast display protein production measurements for the designed scFvs [9].fleishman_destress_data.csv - DE-STRESS metrics [1] for AlphaFold2 models of the designed scFvs (five models per design).pdb_destress_data.csv - DE-STRESS metrics for 35 experimentally determined scFv structures from the Structural Antibody Database (SAbDab) [10, 11].scfv_pdb_list.txt - PDB IDs of the SAbDab scFv structures [10, 11].

Not included

The AlphaFold DB and PDB structure files, the AlphaFold2 models of the designed scFvs, and the full AFDB cluster membership table are not included. The first two are public (AlphaFold DB: https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk/download; PDB: https://www.rcsb.org), and the cluster table is available from https://afdb-cluster.steineggerlab.workers.dev/. The list of AlphaFold DB proteome archives used is in the GitHub repository (`src/data_download/afdb_proteome_index.html`).

 

References

[1] Stam, Michael J., and Christopher W. Wood. 2021. ‘DE-STRESS: A User-Friendly Web Application for the Evaluation of Protein Designs’. Protein Engineering, Design and Selection 34 (February): gzab029. https://doi.org/10.1093/protein/gzab029.

[2] Jumper, John, Richard Evans, Alexander Pritzel, et al. 2021. ‘Highly Accurate Protein Structure Prediction with AlphaFold’. Nature 596 (7873): 7873. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-021-03819-2.

[3] Varadi, Mihaly, Stephen Anyango, Mandar Deshpande, et al. 2022. ‘AlphaFold Protein Structure Database: Massively Expanding the Structural Coverage of Protein-Sequence Space with High-Accuracy Models’. Nucleic Acids Research 50 (D1): D439–44. https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gkab1061.

[4] Berman, Helen M., John Westbrook, Zukang Feng, et al. 2000. ‘The Protein Data Bank’. Nucleic Acids Research 28 (1): 235–42. https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/28.1.235.

[5] Barrio-Hernandez, Inigo, Jingi Yeo, Jürgen Jänes, et al. 2023. ‘Clustering Predicted Structures at the Scale of the Known Protein Universe’. Nature 622 (7983): 637–45. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-06510-w.

[6] The UniProt Consortium. 2023. ‘UniProt: The Universal Protein Knowledgebase in 2023’. Nucleic Acids Research 51 (D1): D523–31. https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gkac1052.

[7] Schoch, Conrad L., Stacy Ciufo, Mikhail Domrachev, et al. 2020. ‘NCBI Taxonomy: A Comprehensive Update on Curation, Resources and Tools’. Database 2020 (January): baaa062. https://doi.org/10.1093/database/baaa062.

[8] Smith, Martin R. 2020. ‘Information Theoretic Generalized Robinson–Foulds Metrics for Comparing Phylogenetic Trees’. Bioinformatics 36 (20): 5007–13. https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btaa614.

[9] Baran, Dror, M. Gabriele Pszolla, Gideon D. Lapidoth, et al. 2017. ‘Principles for Computational Design of Binding Antibodies’. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 114 (41): 10900–10905. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1707171114.

[10] Dunbar, James, Konrad Krawczyk, Jinwoo Leem, et al. 2014. ‘SAbDab: The Structural Antibody Database’. Nucleic Acids Research 42 (Database issue): D1140–46. https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gkt1043.

[11] Schneider, Constantin, Matthew I. J. Raybould, and Charlotte M. Deane. 2022. ‘SAbDab in the Age of Biotherapeutics: Updates Including SAbDab-Nano, the Nanobody Structure Tracker’. Nucleic Acids Research 50 (D1): D1368–72. https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gkab1050.

titles.title: Neither AlphaFold3 confidence nor Boltz-2 affinity measures substrate discrimination in threonyl-tRNA synthetase: data, code and manuscript

affiliation: Department of Chemistry and Physics, McNeese State University, Lake Charles, LA, USA
creators.name: Boggavarapu, Kiran

descriptions.description:
Complete data, code and manuscript for the preprint of the same title. Contains AlphaFold3 and Boltz-2 predictions, derived per-sample tables, measured kinetics, analysis code and a self-checking reproduce.py that regenerates every number reported in the paper using the Python standard library alone.
What it shows. (1) Across 18 non-cognate amino acids, no AlphaFold3 confidence observable tracks the published substrate discrimination factors of threonyl-tRNA synthetase; against the binding-step component all three take the wrong sign. (2) They track residue volume instead (rho = -0.58 to -0.63), and controlling for volume leaves nothing behind, so the scores read steric similarity to the cognate rather than discrimination. Serine, the non-cognate this enzyme rejects best at the binding step, scores highest of all 18. (3) A trained affinity head (Boltz-2, 5 seeds) behaves differently: correct sign in 5 seeds of 5 (rho = +0.470 against I-prime, p at 0.05; rho = -0.600 against D for the binder probability, p = 0.009) and no steric confound (rho against volume -0.140; partial correlation given volume undiminished at +0.458). It still does not resolve discrimination, ranking serine 11th of 18 and placing cysteine and tryptophan above the cognate. (4) Neither readout is blind to catalysis: alanine-substituting the three zinc ligands collapses the threonine-over-valine preference by 0.112 (95% CI 0.106-0.117) and inverts it, with no change in predicted fold.
Measured discrimination factors are transcribed with attribution from Freist, Sternbach & Cramer (1994) Eur J Biochem 220:745-752, doi:10.1111/j.1432-1033.1994.tb18675.x. Residue volumes from Zamyatnin (1972) Prog Biophys Mol Biol 24:107-123. Boltz-2 from Passaro et al. (2025), doi:10.1101/2025.06.14.659707.
reproduce.py runs on the Python standard library alone and self-checks 38 reported values against the shipped figure source data.

titles.title: Structure-prediction confidence detects an enzyme's catalytic site but does not measure how well it discriminates: data, code and manuscript

affiliation: Department of Chemistry and Physics, McNeese State University, Lake Charles, LA, USA
creators.name: Boggavarapu, Kiran

descriptions.description:
Complete data, code and manuscript for the preprint of the same title. Contains the AlphaFold3 predictions, derived per-sample tables, measured kinetics, analysis code and a self-checking reproduce.py that regenerates every number reported in the paper using the Python standard library alone.
Two results. (2) The same scores are not blind to the structure: substituting the three zinc-binding residues with alanine collapses the threonine-over-valine preference by 0.112 (95% CI 0.106-0.117) and inverts it, without changing the predicted fold. titles.title: GenPept-Curated-2025: An annotation-derived, high-identity-controlled benchmark for antimicrobial peptide annotation prediction

affiliation: Faculty of Information Technology, Ho Chi Minh City University of Natural Resources and Environment, 236B Le Van Sy, Tan Son Hoa, Ho Chi Minh City 700000, Viet Nam; Faculty of Information Technology, HUTECH University, 475A Dien Bien Phu, Thanh My Tay, Ho Chi Minh City 700000, Vietnam
creators.name: Pham, Huynh Trong

affiliation: School of Innovation, Design and Technology, Wellington Institute of Technology, 21 Kensington Avenue, Lower Hutt 5012, New Zealand
creators.name: Nguyen-Vo, Thanh-Hoang

affiliation: Faculty of Information Technology, HUTECH University, 475A Dien Bien Phu, Thanh My Tay, Ho Chi Minh City 700000, Vietnam
creators.name: Huynh, Bao

descriptions.description:
Overview

GenPept-Curated-2025 version 1.1 is an annotation-derived, sequence-level benchmark of 11,000 unique GenPept/NCBI Protein sequences for binary antimicrobial-peptide (AMP) annotation prediction.

Scientific purpose

The dataset supports reproducible evaluation of machine-learning methods that predict AMP annotation from peptide or short protein sequences. Its balanced benchmark design and fixed partitions provide a common basis for method comparison.

Data source

Sequences were retrieved from GenPept/NCBI Protein molecular sequence resources, covering Bacteria, Archaea and Fungi and sequence lengths of 10–200 amino-acid residues. Preserved operational NCBI query specifications for the main and precursor-related source queries are included in the package.

Dataset construction

The documented construction workflow uses IPG-based deduplication, annotation-based labeling, and CD-HIT clustering at 90% pairwise sequence identity, followed by cluster-intact partitioning and post-split MMseqs2 verification. The released canonical CSV contains 11,000 distinct sequences. In this release, sequence_clean equals sequence and len_clean equals length for every record. The synchronized public release preserves the final canonical dataset, direct split subsets, construction and benchmark reproduction sources, manuscript figures, environment documentation and scientific QA/provenance. Packaging synchronization does not change scientific sequences, labels, partitions, source cells or meaningful saved outputs.

Class definition

AMP identifies records with qualifying AMP annotations under the documented operational labeling rules. The non-AMP label identifies annotation-negative/unlabeled comparison records: absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. These comparison records are not experimentally confirmed inactive peptides. Labels are annotation-derived rather than uniform assay-defined outcomes.

Dataset composition

There are 11,000 records: 5,500 AMP annotation-positive records and 5,500 annotation-negative/unlabeled comparison records. There are 11,000 unique sequences and 11,000 unique sample IDs. The 50:50 composition is a controlled benchmark design and is not an estimate of natural AMP prevalence. Sequence lengths range from 10 to 200 amino-acid residues.

Train/validation/test partition

The authoritative split field assigns 7,700 records to train (3,850 per class), 990 to validation, encoded as val (495 per class), and 2,310 to test (1,155 per class). The convenience files data/splits/train.csv, data/splits/validation.csv and data/splits/test.csv are exact direct subsets of the canonical split field and do not define alternative partitions.

High-identity and component leakage control

Partition control is component-aware: the 10,666 released operational connected components, identified by comp_id, do not cross the canonical partitions. The preserved MMseqs2 audit summary reports zero cross-partition matches under its reported settings of at least 90% identity and at least 0.8 coverage of the shorter sequence. This is a report of the preserved audit, not a newly executed sequence-similarity search. CD-HIT and MMseqs2 operational screens have different implementations and their definitions are not interchangeable. High-identity control does not establish universal remote-homology independence, biological-family independence, or absence of every possible source of information leakage. comp_id is an operational partition-control identifier, not a biological-family annotation.

Canonical dataset

The authoritative file is data/GenPept_Curated_2025_primary_split_v1.1.csv. Its SHA-256 is bdfe03fbabbd0c7d6ff95ff42905680bb86ad0056e24cf964a33598aefb407a2. The release version is 1.1. Older dataset.csv, balanced_11000.csv or legacy split artifacts must not be substituted for this canonical public dataset.

Package contents

The single official archive is GenPept-Curated-2025_ZENODO_DATASET_v1.1_Final.zip (SHA-256: 4abd28850e4b89cd96ed9ea7e63034b4c8923eae13a607744db2448e7ff58e3f). Its 40 files match the relative paths and bytes published in GitHub main and tag v1.1 at commit 8c52bd73dc5f2d14877e5f4bcc0bdabeeeb1234e and the GitHub Release v1.1 asset. Contents include canonical data and direct splits; dataset-construction and benchmark reproduction sources; manuscript figures; environment documentation; docs/DATA_DICTIONARY.csv; docs/SOURCE_AND_RIGHTS.md; ZENODO_METADATA.md; preserved provenance and validation records; MANIFEST.csv; and SHA256SUMS.txt. The existing DOI and version 1.1 are retained.

Intended use

Use train for model fitting, val for model selection and validation, and the fixed test partition for final evaluation. Report preprocessing, sequence representation, model hyperparameters, random seeds, decision-threshold selection and evaluation metrics. Retain the released split for direct benchmark comparisons. The dataset supports research on sequence-based annotation prediction; it does not establish experimental antimicrobial activity for individual sequences.

Limitations

Annotation-derived labels may reflect the source annotation process. The comparison class is not an experimentally validated inactive class. Sequence length, source annotation and taxonomic structure can carry predictive information. The canonical test set is an in-benchmark holdout with operational high-identity control; it is not a prospective, temporal, taxonomic, biological-family-held-out or clinical cohort. The canonical public CSV does not retain accession, taxonomy, original annotation text, IPG, precursor or other source metadata absent from its documented columns. Row-level source provenance cannot be reconstructed from fields that are not present.

Reproducibility information

The package includes the preserved executable NCBI query specifications, a column dictionary, QA and integrity summaries, a manifest with file sizes and SHA-256 hashes, package checksums, and a portable Python standard-library validator. Run python validate_dataset.py from the extracted release directory to check canonical identity, record and class counts, sequence properties, component separation and exact split subsets. The provided validator does not rerun source retrieval, CD-HIT or MMseqs2. Distinguish reproducibility of the documented retrieval and curation rules from row-level provenance available in the public CSV. Cite the Zenodo DOI of the exact dataset version used; any associated article DOI is a separate related identifier.

License and source rights

Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0; SPDX: CC-BY-4.0) applies to creator-owned curation, operational labels and derived annotations, split assignments, documentation, validation metadata and compilation, only to the extent the creators hold the relevant copyright or database rights. This statement does not claim ownership of, or purport to relicense, third-party rights in underlying NCBI/GenBank sequence records. As explained in docs/SOURCE_AND_RIGHTS.md, NCBI states that it places no restrictions on use or distribution of molecular data in its databases, while original submitters or jurisdictions may claim patent, copyright or other rights that NCBI cannot grant. Users remain responsible for respecting applicable source-record rights. See https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/home/about/policies/, https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/genbank/about/ and https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/.

The authoritative split field assigns 7,700 records to train (3,850 per class), 990 to validation, encoded as val (495 per class), and 2,310 to test (1,155 per class). The convenience files data/splits/train.csv, data/splits/validation.csv and data/splits/test.csv are exact direct subsets of the canonical split field and do not define alternative partitions.

High-identity and component leakage control

Partition control is component-aware: the 10,666 released operational connected components, identified by comp_id, do not cross the canonical partitions. The preserved MMseqs2 audit summary reports zero cross-partition matches under its reported settings of at least 90% identity and at least 0.8 coverage of the shorter sequence. This is a report of the preserved audit, not a newly executed sequence-similarity search. CD-HIT and MMseqs2 operational screens have different implementations and their definitions are not interchangeable. High-identity control does not establish universal remote-homology independence, biological-family independence, or absence of every possible source of information leakage. comp_id is an operational partition-control identifier, not a biological-family annotation.

Canonical dataset

The authoritative file is data/GenPept_Curated_2025_primary_split_v1.1.csv. Its SHA-256 is bdfe03fbabbd0c7d6ff95ff42905680bb86ad0056e24cf964a33598aefb407a2. The release version is 1.1. Older dataset.csv, balanced_11000.csv or legacy split artifacts must not be substituted for this canonical public dataset.

Package contents

The single official archive is GenPept-Curated-2025_ZENODO_DATASET_v1.1_Final.zip (SHA-256: 4abd28850e4b89cd96ed9ea7e63034b4c8923eae13a607744db2448e7ff58e3f). Its 40 files match the relative paths and bytes published in GitHub main and tag v1.1 at commit 8c52bd73dc5f2d14877e5f4bcc0bdabeeeb1234e and the GitHub Release v1.1 asset. Contents include canonical data and direct splits; dataset-construction and benchmark reproduction sources; manuscript figures; environment documentation; docs/DATA_DICTIONARY.csv; docs/SOURCE_AND_RIGHTS.md; ZENODO_METADATA.md; preserved provenance and validation records; MANIFEST.csv; and SHA256SUMS.txt. The existing DOI and version 1.1 are retained.

Intended use

Use train for model fitting, val for model selection and validation, and the fixed test partition for final evaluation. Report preprocessing, sequence representation, model hyperparameters, random seeds, decision-threshold selection and evaluation metrics. Retain the released split for direct benchmark comparisons. The dataset supports research on sequence-based annotation prediction; it does not establish experimental antimicrobial activity for individual sequences.

Limitations

Annotation-derived labels may reflect the source annotation process. The comparison class is not an experimentally validated inactive class. Sequence length, source annotation and taxonomic structure can carry predictive information. The canonical test set is an in-benchmark holdout with operational high-identity control; it is not a prospective, temporal, taxonomic, biological-family-held-out or clinical cohort. The canonical public CSV does not retain accession, taxonomy, original annotation text, IPG, precursor or other source metadata absent from its documented columns. Row-level source provenance cannot be reconstructed from fields that are not present.

Reproducibility information

The package includes the preserved executable NCBI query specifications, a column dictionary, QA and integrity summaries, a manifest with file sizes and SHA-256 hashes, package checksums, and a portable Python standard-library validator. Run python validate_dataset.py from the extracted release directory to check canonical identity, record and class counts, sequence properties, component separation and exact split subsets. The provided validator does not rerun source retrieval, CD-HIT or MMseqs2. Distinguish reproducibility of the documented retrieval and curation rules from row-level provenance available in the public CSV. Cite the Zenodo DOI of the exact dataset version used; any associated article DOI is a separate related identifier.

This statement does not claim ownership of, or purport to relicense, third-party rights in underlying NCBI/GenBank sequence records. As explained in docs/SOURCE_AND_RIGHTS.md, NCBI states that it places no restrictions on use or distribution of molecular data in its databases, while original submitters or jurisdictions may claim patent, copyright or other rights that NCBI cannot grant. Users remain responsible for respecting applicable source-record rights. See https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/home/about/policies/, https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/genbank/about/ and https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/.
